div.p: SEEM
ANIMAL CHARCOAL AND COLOUR.

The curious fact that while animal char- coal will remove the colouring matter from coloured liquids, ordinary charcoal will not, has long been known. The cause of this dif- ference, however, was not apparent. Recent investigations seem to shew that it is due to the presence of nitrogen in the charcoal made from bones. It has been shewn that animal charcoal contains from 5 to 7 per cent., while wood charcoal contains none. And as the nitrogen is gradually eliminated from the animal charcoal its decolourising effects are reduced in proportion.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Mr. Keir Hardie and the Bova Garden Party.—Mr. and Mrs. John Burns were among those honoured with invitations to the State Pail at Blickimeham Palace. Such an invitation would issue as a matter of ceurse to a Cabinet Minister, bet time nes when Mr. Burns would have as little expected to go to Buckingham Palace, as air. Keir Iliadic., who hes taken exception to his exclusion from the invitations to the recent Garden Party at Windsor CeetTe. The members of Parliament with w hem Nr. Eeir Hardie usually acts, received invitntions but, it being &sauteed that Mr. Keir Hardie was excluded for political rev-roes the Labour repre- sentatives have requested that all their names should be removed from the Lord Chamberlain's list. That action e ould appear to to in perticularly bad taste in view of the explanation that the reason why Mr. Kerr Ilardie was net invited wets because he had previously received similar invitatiene, but had contemptuously . returned or refused them, and had publicly declared that he bad no intention of going to any Royal enter- tainment whatever. The London Season.—The State Ball at Buckingham , Palace last week, concluded the Court functions for the : season. The King has lorg since given up taking any active part in the dancing on snch cccasiors, and his Majesty, and the Queen merely lead the way in the opening Royal quire:rifle, only ore figure of which is danced. The Princess of Wales on the other hand is a keen dancer,like her brothers Prince Frances and Prince • Alexander of Teck,—and usually misses but few of the waltzes. Amon the younger Royalties present were Princess Patricia of Connaught, her dater the Crown Princess of Sweden, acid the Hereditary Princess of liolienlotre-Langenhurg, who all kept up the dancing with great energy. In all, over 2,0(.0 goests were present, a great many of whom are now leasing Lendon and will seen be ecattered about at the seaside and -various health resorts at home end abroad. Goodwood -and Cowes Regatta, ere the only remaining great at tractions for fashionable society, lifter which the King will follow his usual practice and leave for Marienhad about the middle o f August for his custcmary three week's cure. The Dowager Duchess of Devenshire.—Compton Place, Eastbourne, where the Downger Duchess of Devonshire has taken up her residence, is an ideal dower house. Situated at the foot of the downs, a mile or so from the sea, this pretty creeper-covered mansion nestles within its walled gardens, which by the way are beautifully kept rp, and a blaze of colour just now. In tne luxuriently fitted stables may be seen the famous herd of Dexter cattle, in which the Duchess is so greatly interested, and with which she has carried off so many prizes. Since the death of the late Duke of Devonshire, the health of the Dowager Duchess has occasioned her friends some concern, and with the first touch of autumn there is to be a family flitting to Egypt or the Riviera. The Scheel Etaminations.—This is the season when the dread ordeal of examinations confronts the youth- fin l mind. In many households it is also a time of maxiety for parents, who are bitterly disappointed if their own darling is not first in everything. To them, a bad report from school comes as a terrible blow and it is little use pointing cut to them the wisdom of not taking things too seriously. They ehould however, recceraber that the elements of art and luck usually count for something at examinations, and it is very often the Case that the most successful in life are those who have not always had the best reperts from echoed. The Eton and Darrow Match.—There are few more fashionable gatherings than the society picnic for which the Eton and Harrow cricket match proviees an excuse, and at which the three young Princes of Wales were among the lookers-en. It is an event in which sisters and cousins shew a great deal of partisan enthusiasm, whilst parents reminded of their own youth, sumptu- ously entertain the young folks, and look on with all the interest of those who have seas at one or other of the schools. Unfortunately the bad weather rather spoiled the show of dainty frocks and finery, and the one sided nature of the genie detracted somewhat from interest in the match. It is sometimes said that whilst girls are becoming more runsculine in their ways, boss ere becoming more effircinate. Eton and Harrow would no doutt resent such an insinuation, although only the other day the- headmaster of liarrew deplored the frequency with wh'cli mothers ring up to make tsl3- phone enquiries, or call in a motor to take their boys for an outing. With the nowadays usual small family, parents are apt to fuss over their children perhaps more than used to te the case, and if so, there is some dancer that it will develop qualities in boys which are not to be admired. Athletic Games and Small Waists.—As might b 3 anpposed, the fashionable corsetreres are not in favour of young girls irelnigiog in athletic games and physical exercise. To attain the conspicuously slender waist, the stay lace must he brought early into use, and that is impossible if girls will go boating and cycling, and play hockey, tennis, cricket, and so on. As a conse- quence the average n easurements of hands, feet, and waists show it tendency to increase, and this is held up as the price which girls must pay for their indulgence in athletic games. There is lie doubt a good deal of ; truth in all this, but the active and healthy life has its ' compensations, and the modern girl shows her setse in preferring to enjoy these benefits rather than sacrifice ranch for the remote possibility of one day being the cynosure of all eyes in the drawing-room. Bathing Dress More Simple.—Generally speaking bathing dress is more simple than it has been for several yeara past. There are, of course, numbers of girls and women who make sea bathing (?) an excuse for es-wiring startling and wonderful costumes, fascinating hats, end dainty shoes and stockings. hut the majority ! are donning simple dresses, of the Princess variety— such as are sePn at the Bath Club in London on ladies' days—and taking bathing and swimming seriousiy. A very favourite fabric for bathing dress this summer is vyelta, which does not cling any more closely to the lie,nre than does serge, end is of course much softer. Alpaca hag a certain vogue, so also has hopsack, while black silk costumes trimmed with white, or tartan bends are exploited by smart "bobbers." Concerning wraps to be worn when leaving tho sea for the tent, those built of red and cream striped Turhish towelling are undoubtedly best. These pcielloire aro provided with long wide sleeves, also hoods, which can be gathered up with a running siring. And with regard to the smart little caps so many of us are wearing over besiness-like waterproof ones, we shceld take care that the colours and absolutely "safe" and fixed, otherwise a striped complexion and one difficult to remove, may result. The Hands in Strnmer.—The open air girl or woman who never dreams in slimmer of wearing gloves when walking about the country, sitting in the garden, or playing outdoor games, needs of course to take a little extra care of her hands ,jest now. A cut lemon should always find a place npc,n the washstand and be used frequently after trashing the hands, also a little good cream, or a mix I tire of three earls of glycerine and one of rose water, which should he well rubbed in at night, the last thing before retiring. In the uncomfortable prickly rash upon the hands and arms, from which AO many of ns are suffering this snrnmer, few soothers equal horseradish-cream. The horseradish is grated or scraped into a little cream, and set aside for a few hours, in a cool place. The liquid is then strained cff, and can be lightly dabbed upon the affected pens with a soft little brush, or a tiny sponge, and left to dry in. Good for the Complexion.—Equel quantities of orange and lemon juice, squeezed into a tablespoon and taken the fleet thing upon rising in the morning, are excellent for the complexion. No water should be added cr sugar,

div.head: PRETTY Baows COSTUMES.
div.p: PRETTY Baows COSTUMES.

At every great outdoor gathering during th:s function-crowded season, says "Madge" in Truth, there have been two or three successful brown costumes which have evoked criticism pro and con. One of these was in copper-brown mus- lin with golden-brown straw hat and many cop- pery feathers standing up like sleepy, drooping sentries round the crown. Another was in the exact tone of an autumn laurel leaf, in very fine cloth. It suited beautifully the clear complexion and dark auburn hair of the very pretty wearer.

div.head: DATNTY NICIITGOWN.
div.p: A DATNTY NICIITGOWN.

Pictured in our sketch is 4, delightfully pretty and simple little nightgown, just the thing for warm weather wear. This dainty little nightie is extremely simple in shape, and requires but the minimum of making, for there are no fasten- ings on either sleeves or gown. The neck is cut out in a round decolletage, and the edgo finished Try a simple scallop and spot pattern, below

which are worked slots through which ribbon is threaded, and drawn up to make the night- gown fit comfortably about the .shoulders. This scallop and simple design are very easily man- aged by even an inexperienced embroidreso, and as they add immensely to the chic effect of the garment are well worth the time and trouble they involve. The sleeves are plain bell-shaped affairs, lust long enough to cover the elbow, and are finished by an embroidered scallop to match the neck. _ _

div.head: TEE SAPIENT MITE.
div.p: TEE SAPIENT MITE.

Not all women who attend sales know how, when, and what to buy, declares a writer in M.A.P. There 'is one who has a huge ottoman- couch in her bedroom piled high and running over with odds and ends for which she will never find a use. She bought them, not because she needed them or saw possibilities in them, but because they were cheap. Another woman, with a reputation for being always well and ex- pensively turned out, owes it -to the fact that she has a definite aim in view every time she spends a shilling. Beautiful " bits " of embroi- dery, pieces of good silk, satin, and vel*at, a few yards of fine muslin, are among the, things that appeal to her, and later they emerge upon even- ing dresses; as petticoats, tea jackets, theatre wraps; and as frocks for the children. Decay- ing finery does not interest her, but cottons, linens and serges, coats, and the like, that can be worn in the country or at the seaside later on, as well as hose and a certain amount of foot- wear, she will buy. Furs she touches with ex- ceeding caution, as the fashions vary so greatly from year to year. Now and then a really good model gown, that perhaps needs cleaning before it can be worn, falls to her at a price that ren- ders it worth while.

div.head: METEOR TRAINS.
div.p: METEOR TRAINS.

Professor C. C. Trowbridge says that teor trains are the luminous clouds formed by meteors which persist long after the incandescent body has disappeared. The average of the heights above the earth's sur- face of the middle portion of the trains is fifty-four miles, the minimum being about forty-five miles, and the maximum sixty- five miles. It would thus appear that in the zone between fifty and sixty miles altitude there exist the special atmcspheric condi- tions necessary for the production of these phenomena.
ROW NATURAL MAGNETS ARE MADE.

Magnetised places -- spots attracting iron like the lodestone—are often noticed in vol- canic rocks. They have been ascribed by Folgheraiter to lightning, but he knew of no magnetised rocks that had been tested be- fore the lightning struck. An instance has now been described. Two investigator's had been testing rocks near Mount Etna, when, during a September night, lightning fused a telephone wire from which an uninsulated earth wire ran along a basaltic wall, which had previously shown scarcely a trace of magnetism: Next morning the stones of the wall were strongly magnetic fcr sin. on both sides of the wire, the polarity indicating that the current linseed upwards.

div.head: EDIBLE SEAWEEDS OF HAWAII.
div.p: THE EDIBLE SEAWEEDS OF HAWAII.

There are upivarcls of seventy species of edible seaweeds growing on the coasts of Hawaii, and about forty of these are in cora: mon use by the natives. Seeing that Japan derives a large income from the economic utilisation of its alge, it is eusgeeted that the edible seaweeds of Hawaii migat be used in like manner as the raw material for the manufacture of gelatine, glue, starch, ece. At present, says Knowledge, the algm, which are known lecallY as Emu, are only cultivated in a crude fashion, and are chiefly used in the form of salads. They contain a large pro- portion •of phesphates, chlorides, bromides, and iodides, and are rich in starch and other carbo-hydrates. ANOTHER !SOON FOR JUPITER.

Jupiter, already amply provided with satel- lites, has been found to have an eighth. ,The discovery of the new moon illustrates the im- portance of the application of photography to astronomy, for it only revealed itself by a little_ spot on the photographic plate. It is in the same way that minor planets and stars of lesser magnitude have been dis- covered in recent years. It was soon after the inventi6n of the telescope that Galileo d,seovered four of Jupiter's moons. The fifth was found by the American astronomer Bar- nard in 1802, and ths sixth and seventh by Perrine. The latest addition to Jupiter's satellites was discovered by the staff .of the Greenwich Observatory.

div.head: WOMEN CANNOT GUESS TIME.
div.p: WOMEN CANNOT GUESS TIME.

An experiment has' been made by Pro- feesor MacDo32 uaall the results indicating _t that woman has no sense of time. The ex- periment was made in the case of 231 young men, ranging in years from seventeen to twenty-three, and 274 girls, between seven- teen and twenty. The actual intervals of time set for calculation were from .16 to 10$ seconds of duration. The tittle guessers were either idle, or engaged in reading or writing. The results shewed that women guess time far less approximately than men, the ten- dency of the female sex being to exaggerate grossly. One, for instance, expressed her seneh: of the duration of one minute and a. half as being of quite ten minutes. The men fell usually below the exact duration of time, though not much.

div.head: SCIENTIFIC SUNDIAL.
div.p: THE SCIENTIFIC SUNDIAL.

In modern use the sundial is chiefly an ornament, as the ordinary instrument re- quires troublesome calculations to shew any- thing like true time, and it can be consulted only during hours of sunshine. The photo- heliometer shewn at the .soirée of the Lon- don Royal Society is en improved sundial giving direct time readings with sufficient precision for regulating common clocks and watches. It consists essentially of a ball-and- socket stand for adjustments in latitude and level, an hour circle which can slide round to follow the apparent motion of the sun, and a year circle on which are engraved the months. Greenwich mean time is indicated when the hour circle is moved so that the spot of light coming through an upper screen falls on the eentral line. The year circle is turned to _indicate the current day and month, and a cam or curved plate on its under side automatically applies the neces- sary corrections.

div.head: CURIOUS EXPERIMENT.
div.p: A CURIOUS EXPERIMENT.

Major B. Baden-Powell, in a practical book he has written on ballooning, mentions a curiotts little experiment which may be made when it becomes desirable to throw out ballast. A • piece of newspaper about a foot square is laid out flat and heaped with a double handful .of sand. It is then carefully lifted by its four corners and dropped over. As it falls the cornets of the Faper begin to flap, and as the speed augments the flapping becomes more rapid and noisy till it makes a shrill rattle. Then as the pace of the de- scent _becomes_ very_ great the pressure below the paper becomes so excessive that the paper suddenly bursts, and the sand, dispers- ing into a cloud, gives just the appearance of a bursting shell. This system of discharg• lug ballast has its uses, too, for when one is descending rapidly the sand that is thrown out loosely falls more slowly than the bal- loon, so that the aeronauts are smothered with dust. Thrown out on paper the sand falls quicker than the balloen, and is dis- persed below. Major Baden-Powell adds a caution against taking moist sand ballast. At great heights it becomes frozen. Very often the discharge of a mere handful of bal- last is sufficient to send the balloon upwards again after it has been falling.

div.head: OLD TESTAMENT CHEMISTRY.
div.p: OLD TESTAMENT CHEMISTRY.

Professor Pinner, a celebrated chemist, who has been studying the knowledge of chemistry which the ancient Hebrews pos- sessed.as manifested by the writers of the Old Testament, concludes that they knew only the first elements of chemistry, such as the barbarous peoples of to-day are ac- quainted with. He says that the Egyptian priests with whom Moses came in contact were chemists of no mean order, but they kept to themselves what they kn?sv,. and cer- tainly ,did not impart it to the leaders of their Jewish captives and slaves. Professor Pinner quotes the long list of articles named in the second chapter of Ezekiel, and says it shews that the Israelites depended on other nations for articles in whose manufacture a knowledge of chemistry was needed. Thus the Phoenicians made the metal work for the Temple. There is an interesting passage in Jeremiah—" For though thou wash thee with nitre and take thee much soap," &e. The word here rendered "nitre," says Pro- fessor Pinner, should be soda, and that translated " soap " should be potash. In making bricks by primitive methods the Hebrews preferred red clay to white because 16 is Louguer. ‘v bac clay is more porous, and the Jews, even as late as Solomon's time, did not know how to glaze bricks.—Popular Science BiftingB.

div.head: SHATTERED DREAM.
div.p: A SHATTERED DREAM.
BY MABEL COLLINS, it utlior of "Lady Ladelle of Mere House," "Almost Trapped," "A Dead Love," &e.

Mrs. Ifolroyd came into my life for a very brief time, only for two months, yet in that time I saw her most cherished dream shattered, the dream that had made her existence bearable. Poor little thing, she was so pretty, and so gay, and with such a romantic look in her great blue eyes when I first saw her. Later on I saw those eyes full of nothing but terror—terror at the inexorable blow Which fell and shattered her dream. She came one morning to look at my cottage, intending to take it for two months. It stands on a cliff by the sea, and in the summer I often let it and go awax to something different—forests, or moors, or lats. Mrs. Holroyd was sent by a house-agent to look at it. ,She had come down from London and was determined to find a house quickly, for she had a dinner-party in the evening and was anxious to get back in time to dress for it. So the house-agent sent her first to my cottage, which he felt sure would please her. And it did; she desired to go no further. Bat she was altogether too quick for me. lam an old maid, and like -to take my time and think about things a little before I do them. She wanted_ the house immediately, and I could not bring myself to hurry off like that, so she took one a few yards from mine, just separated by a garden plot, and drove off to the station nytime to catch her' train. -

"Nothing like so pretty a house as yours, 'Miss Millet,". she said, stopping at the gate for a moment to tell me about it ;"but I cannot look any further. I must be home in time for dinner. friend is cuming who is just home from South .Africa. I cotthenot disappoint him by being late. Besides, it is quite a dinner-party, and 1 hare sereral important gnests.". But it was the 'friend just home from South Africa" that mattered.

He was a handsome young officer invalided home. . He came down a few • days after she and her daughter and her daughter's governess, and her r .tinne of servants had established themselves as my neighbours, and he remained as part of the estahlishmert. I decided not to let my cottage at all that year, and I Was quite as much amused as I should have been in any new place. Mrs. Holroyd was a widow, just laying aside her weeds. She told me in the early days of our acquaintance that her husband had been much older than herself, , that in fact it had been a marriage of convenience. She had gratified • a dying mother's wish by marrying a very rich man. But she •made nse understand that she would not have done this had she not believed that her chosen lover, the man of her heart, had forgotten her. She had since found that this was not, so; that he was as true as ever ; and the light in her blue eyes told me that he was none other than the "friend just home from South Africa "—Captain Steyne, My quiet, old-maidish cottage was the scene of many interesting interviews 'and confidences. Mrs. Holroyd had taken a fancy to ma, and she used to run adross the garden at all hours to tell me bits of news or talk over arrangements with me. She 'came sometimes in the lessening,' in delicate cambric wrappers, her pretty Bair loosely twisted up, looking like a girl in her teens—her dafighter's sister: She came in her bicycling dress, in her yachting dress, in her smart dresses for the concerts or the promenade, , and in each and all I thought her simply lovely. She had a yacht in the bay, but he only used it for luncheon parties, to which she /tried. to induce me, to go; but I was a bad sailer, and preferred to lunch at home alone and hear her account of the lunch on board the yacht when she came back from it. She was one of those people who always have adventures, and never come back fresh an hour's absence without a story to relete. Captain Steyne sometimes waited for her at the gate, leaning on it and watching the door till she came out like a faithful dog. Sometimes he came in and set and listened to her, watchiNe her all the time with the •deepest interest and admiration. He was a fine fellow, quiet, soldierly, and gentlemanly. He had been badly wounded, but had got over the worst of his illness in hospital in South _Africa, and was recovering his health and spirits. But I was troubled about one thin. She had married a man leech older than herself, she would not amend that mistake by now marrying a man younger than herself. For this he was, though they had been playfellows as children and boy and girl sweethearts. Her daughter, Una, just seventeen, was far better suited to Captain Steyno. I saw this from the first, and my heart sank at the trouble I saw on ahead for my bright new friend. But it was a very long way off. Captain Steyne had no eyes for anyone but his old sweet- heart. I'saw very little of Una Holroyd. Her governess was also her friend, and the two went off for long bicycle rides or long walks together, and were seldom at home, except at dinner in the evening. Of course, they went to the yacht luncheons and the picnics, but, then, I would net be cajoled into taking part in these. I am not fond of tiring myself to the verge of an illness, and calling it pleasure. How they enjoyed themselves, all these happy young people! How gay they were! Mrs. Holroyd in her pretty black-and-white dresses looked not a young widow so much Es a young girl. Una regarded her very seriously sometimes when she was gayest; and occasionally I fancied I saw a glance as of reproach. But it was not easy to be spre; the girl was of a different nature.from her soother, quiet, reserved, serious, and poetical. She was deeply read in poetry, and I learnt by an accident that site wrote it. She will be famous by-and-! ye, I am told. At this time she was simply very young, and very beanti Cul. Beside her her lovely mother could only be called pretty. Una was a bed opening on to the world, a ereat bud like that of an Annunciation lily ; while Mrs. Holroyd was a full-blown rose, with all its petals unfurled. None were curling up or drooping yet, but I saw a change come upon them. The merry voices came on the soft evening breeze as the party from the next door cottage came_up the path over the cliff night after night, and I smiled to myself over my quiet knitting. I like my solitude, but it snakes it brighter to hear other people so gay and happy. I would lean forward in my rocking-chair and look at the figures as they passed ; how well I knew them now. Two were always together—Mrs. Holroyd and Captain Stesne, who, if he could not hold her hand or give her his arm, followed her like her shadow. It was almost the end °Utile first month that a sad accident occurred to my dear, pretty little friend. She had organised a wonderful picnic away up in the country which involved a long drive through lanes. It was not a very good journey for bicyclists as there were some sharp hill's, but most of the party preferred cycling to driving: " They were talking it over on the previous evening at my gate, and Captain Steyne turned and appealed to me. "Miss Millet," he said, "I believe you have more influence with Mrs. Holroyd than anyone else, including myself. Do beg her to go in the waggonette to-morrow. It is too far for her to cycle." "The waggonette I ' laughed Mrs. HolroS•d. "The servants and the lunch-baskets can go in that, not 1!" "I don't like it," murmured Captain Steync. "You will make yourself ill. I have a feeling that you will. Pleaee don't, Blanche !" I had never heard him call ber Blanche before. She flushed erimson, but only letighed and made no answer. Una turned and •looked at him smith startled surprise. Evidently else hail never heard him use this name. But it paesed off wit hied any further notice amidst the general chatter and laughter. There were other visitors besides Captain Steyne staying at the Holroyd's, and they had asked some people front another yacht which was in the bay to join them at this picnic, CO it would be quite a large party. I watched them go off the next mornlng, having climbed a bit of higher ground behind my 'cottage in order to see them spin away along the road. Mrs. Holroyd led, looking her very prettiest in white serge and a black hat. Captain Steyne was close beside her.

„.. When they came home it was very, very late. ihe long,. hot day had closed with a still, peaceful evening, and the evening sky WM taking on the deep mght blue when et last I beard the horses' feet. How slowly they were coming! I ran out into the road with a premonition of some mis- fortune. A little white Ilgnie lay on cushions in the waggonette. Mrs. lloiroyd had had an gccident going down one of the hills, so they told me hastily. It was on the return journey, so that fortunately she had not been compelled to drive very far in the pain she was suffering. A doctor had been summoned and was now following them on the hill from the little town. I haired them lift her and put her on to her bed and take oft her pretty dress. She was very brave, and her blue axes did not shew any fear. She, had by. sztd

ittavotton to turn to. She knew a tender heart ftcluid for her, and when this is so much pain can be borne without any extraordinary fortitude. It is loss of love, it is solitude, that requires courage, not mere physical pain. Mrs. Holroyd though i she was suffering very much, but she did no yet know what suffering was. That was to come. The doctor assured her that she was not very much hurt, and that it was only a, question of complete rest for a week or two. So we all set to work to pet her and nurse her, and make the titre pass as cheerfully for her as was in any way possible. She began to enjoy being a spoilt invalid when the first anxiety and distress were over, and she found she was not to be a cripple, or dis- figured, or anything dreadful. The days began to be gay again, with a new character about them; Mrs. Holroyd's room was the centre of attraction; it was always full of flowers and sweet scents,and pretty- things. It was converted into a sort of bower for the time being, and everybody worshipred at the shrine of the beauty who lay helpless there. No one went far filmy; Captain Steyne was absolutely devoted all day long, fetching and carry- ing, bringing new bouquets perpetually, reading aloud, and inventing modes of amusing the invalid. But she needed nothinr, niore than the knowledge of his presence to make the time pass easily. How those blue eyes followed him about! At last ens day the streak of unselfishness which redeemed her character asserted itself, and she declared that everybody should not waste the fine weather indoors becauie she could not go out. Una she said, was looking pale for want of a long ride, and Captain Steyne looked as if lie had had a return of his own illness. They must all go out for a long afternoon. They did so, and I eat with the pretty invalid, and we had tea together, and she chatted away volubly, and told me all sorts of amusing stories. _ .

That day a subtle, nameless -change took place. We were all conscious of it, though no one could have expressed it, I am sure. Every afternoon after that one the others went out together, and sometimes I went in to Mrs. Holroyd, and some- times she said she would sleep. Then she grew restless, and got the doctor to say she might begirt to come down to dinner; and she got out fresh dresses, and looked lovelier than ever. But Una - was blossoming; her face was taking a new look, her colour was weeper and richer than ever, and her eyes darker—they were like Bussian violets beside English wood violets when I compared them with her mother's. She had a natural taste for great sevetity in dress ; and it suited her as nothing else would have done. She still wore black, not yet having laid it aside since her father's death, although she might have done so; and when she cant, to the dinner-table in a plain black silk, with a string of pearls round her neck, she was wonderful to look at, fresh from the sea uir,, and in the glory of her dawning womanhood. I sometimes dined with them, staying on when I had been with Mrs. .Tolroyd during the quiet afternoon; and what a merry dinner-table it always was, and what a perfect little hostess we had! How well she understood making everybody happy and at home What delightful musical evenings there were! Captain Steyne sang well, and Ms. Holroyd was a genius in her brilliant way; and Una played the Violin as few amateurs play it. We used to form a great circle round the room, and Una would take up her stand in the centre; and very soon after the first notes of her violin were heard, a crowd began to gather outside—people strolled up from the other houses and stood near to listen. We were all very happy. And I felt that I phould be desperately lonely when all these bright people had gone away. Mrs. Holrayd bad quite adopted me as an intimate friend, and she begged me to come up to see her in London very soon. When she talked about the future I saw an undercurrent of meaning always ; she was uncertain about it, she did not quite know whether she was going to keep on her house in town or go abroad. I knew she had the vision of a second marriage in her mind; and I know quite well also that the Captain had not spoken. I felt that she wanted him to speak while they were here—a faint sense or anxiety came from her to me when she talked about her plans. Th-re was some idea of going abroad for Una, who wanted opportunities for study, which she could only get upon the Continent. And lina's governess, who was now with them as a friend and companion, wanted to go away to live at home with her own mother. "I hardly know what to do with the child," said Mrs. Holroyd, a little absent, uneasy look coining into the pretty eyes. "I think I must go and live abroad, where she will be able to fill her life with study and music, as she wishes to. I think I can arrange to do that—oh, yes,l think so."

There was someone else in her mind besides herself when she said this. Would that someone else be willing to lire abroad ? n e evening I sat quietly at my solitary supper, having refused to go across to my neighbour's gay dinner-table, and I wondered how I should get on without those merry voices, which were so familiar and friendly, coming to me on the soft, scented air across the garden. The dinner was over, but they still sat at the table, laughing and talking, even more merrily than usual, I thought—if that were possible. The dining-room window opened on to the grass at the side of their house; it was a door, and there were chairs just outside it, where Captain Steyne and any other man who might happen to be there smoked their after-dinner cigars. But to-night-it, was not the men who came out, it was two women and- a man. I rose and went to my window and looked ' across, for this was unuswll, and attracted toy attention. It was late, but the summer night was clear; and I saw that the three persons were Mrs. Holroyd and her daughter and Captain Steyne. They stood together, speaking with great earnestness. Then suddenly I saw Mrs. Holroyd stagger, and step back; she put her hand to her head. Was she ill ? She quickly recovered herself, if so; sge turned to Una and kissed her; then she took Captain Steyne's hand for a moment in hers, and I saw she was speaking earnestly to him. Then she pushed them from her with a pretty, imperious,- dramatic gesture, and, turning away, came quickly across the garden plot and through the gate to me. I- opened my window— she came so uncertainly, and with so faltering a step, yet so hurriedly that I had no time to go to meet her. Never shall I forget the woman that came through that window from the dimness of tha night into the brightness of my lamplit room. She was in full evening dress ; I had never seen her so splendid. She was in white satin veiled with exquisite black lace; her low-necked bodice gleamed with diamonds, they glittered on her fair neck and arms and in the dark clusters of her hair. She must, indeed, have looked beautiful while her face wore its natural appearance, but the dress seemed like some strange masquerade with that ashen face above it, with those quivering white lips, those eyes that seemed colourless and already stifik-en into her head. She put her hand to her head again, and sank into a chair that I guided her to.

"The world has gone from under me," she said, looking up at me with piteous eyes. "I don't understand anything." I waited, and we were quite still for a moment. Then suddenly she Said: "The blow was too .unexpected—it has almost sent me out of my mind; but I behaved all right, thank Heaven for. that! Esther Millet, he is a base and hideous traitor, and I should like to kill him—l feel as if I must kill him!" She rose as she said this, and stood there like a tragedy queen, her face passionate and terrible. Then another thought came suddenly: "But my girl loves him I Una I I must net for her sake ; and he has looked me in the face and said he loved her in return I The world began to rock under my feet as I listened to him, and it isn't steady yet. It never will be. I can't understand it. There's no use in my trying to. How can I ? The absolute opposite of everything I believed. Was it all is dream? Can it have been a dream all the time from the very beginning If so, then it is shattered utterly—and I with it. Yes, dear friend, you may look at me reproachfully, but it is true. lam broken." She sank slowly down into her chair again, and was silent for a long time. The colour did not return to her face. I thought she grew whiter. At last she spoke, but alintst in a whisper: "How shall I get through the wedding! (311, it is hard—hard. I' intend to be brave. I despise weak women. Dear Miss Millet, will you go back with me, and come up to my room with me? I am afraid of Una." - - _

No wonder! Without a word, I accompanied her; and, indeed, I had said no word at all yet. There was nothing I know how to say. I remained silent. But site knew—oh, she knew how my heart ached for her; how I longed to help her, how deeply I felt her sense of loss ; but perhaps more than that I felt her humiliation. Perhaps I felt that more keenly than any other part of the whole misery, and therefore it was no doubt a wise instinct which kept my lips closed. For I really do not feet sure that she felt that at all. She was suffering from a crnek wounded heart, and that pain is so great aria 'Absorbing mat a num none to the pride is not recognised beside it. We got quietly into the house and up to her room without meeting anyone. No doubt the lovers were as anxious to avoid us as we were to avoid them, though for very different reasons; and the

rest-of the party were in the drawing-room at the piano, perfectly unaware of the tragedy of love and woe going on beside them. She would not let me. stay with her or help her to undress. "Go, dear friend," she whispered. "I must be alone and face it. I must face it, and face myself, and face my God." She looked very white and Very solemn as she spoke; her face was the face of a saint at this Moment, and it seemed strange to note the glimmer of the diamonds on her breast—a crucifix would have been more in. keeping. So I had to leave her alone. She pressed my' hand and pushed me gently out, and I heard her lock the door when I had passed through it. Then there was silence. I waited a few moments fearing to hear her weep or fall, but I did, not eien hear" her MOTO. She told me afterwards that she stood like a= • statue there for a long time—she did not know how • long—and then took off her jewels and her beautiful dress and dropped them where she stood, and crept to her bed and lay still there. Her blinds were not drawn and she lay looking at the blueness of the night until the greyness of the' dawn came over it and veiled the stars. And when • the morning light came into her room she rose and picked up her jewels and locked them away in their caee. "Una shall ham o them," she emurmured to herself. "Una shall wear them on her wedding- day." And a bright tear, brighter than any of the. diamonds, dropped into the case with them. Then she picked up her dress 'and hung it away in the werdro're. I went across early next morning on some exenee or other. I found them all still sitting round the table at 'late breakfast, and lazily discussing - plamsfor the day: Mrs. Holroyd eat behind the ,urn, fulfilling her duties as hostess in a simple black dress.. She looked a little pale and tired, that was all, to a general observer. 1 noted 3 deep little line at the side of her mouth which was new, and a dfferent look in her eyes. They were drawn and sunken and were making fresh line's in her pretty-face with every passing moment. She smiled at me, a dint, vague little smile. Dim and vague though it was, it told, me all I .needed tca e,kaowsts: Site had fortght the good fight and was the victor. Hers was the languor of success, not of despair. She joined the others in all they did that day, preferring, evidently, not to be by herself nor yet to be alone with me, who alone knew of the slow bleeding of the wounded heart. Por it was bleeding. No courage could alter that, no victory effaee the fact. She had not parted with a passing fancy or a caprice, but bad endured the shattering of a life-long dream of love and happiness. On'y a few days remained now of their stay in the house next mine, end I spent most of my time amongst them as they were so soon to go. nt-1 the most singular-thing I noticed—the thing that surprised and startled me—was that Captain Steyne's manner wee exactly the seine to Mrs. Holroyd ai it had always been. He was not so mat with her, of course, for he was a great deal with Una; but I began to suspect that his had all along: been the devotion of a very affectionate friendship and nothing eke... He was a brave man think I have forgotten to say that he was a V.o.—and one of the kindest and tenderest natures I have ever met with. I had been full of an anger agtinst him that was positively distressing, to me at first, because I had liked him, so. much ; but it began to fade away as I watched him day after day waiting on Mrs. Hoiroyd, bringing her flowers, fetching her books, doing her errands, with just the sem devotion as of old. And he looked so happy and so perfectly nneobscions of there being anything to or mar the beauty of his happiness. They drove away one fine morning to the station, filling two carriages and leaving the servants to bring all the luggage late? in the day; and Mrs. Holroyd looked as bright as any of Ahem when she waved her hand to me with the others as they passed me. I stood at the gate till the sound of the carriage wheels had quite died away. How quiet it,seerced! I never visited them in London, nor could I go to the wedding, which took place in the autumn. I had to ' close my house and leave my beloved quiet, and go to stay with my married sister in the north of England. She was a clergyman's wife with a crowd of children of all ages, and she wee breaking down under the heasy work of a large, poor parish and the task of clothing and educating ' and feeding all these strong, growing young people on a vc.wy manffleient income. So I had to go to, her and do my best to share her burden. A's with Mrs. Holroyd's very different troubles I found that with lily sister I could not help her in any better.way than by letting her speak out to me and talk things over. That s.eetes to be one great use for old maids, to become good listeners. I don't fancy many of us understand how very useful it is. to sit still and listen to long tales of household' cares, or to stand still beside one of those who are •in the thick of a tragedy and let the .wild- worcia pour forth, or to give all arm to 'old folk who like to totter about and prattle of stale sorrows ; and bscause we don't understand this we fancy we have no vocation. The. listener is always welcome, always can find an empty niche to fill, always ears cetumend a seat at every household table. Few people have time to listen, and fewer still the will. Away in the north country Vicarage, listening to- the children's lessons and the girl's clatter. listening to my sister's taik of trouble ahead and narking anxiety, listening. to my brother-in-lawsx tales of parish difficulties, listening to the hard troubles of the poor who came to the house to tell of their griefs and pains—amidst all this I looked ea erly for an occasional note from 'Blanche Holroyd. They had been to Paris to get Ura'se -dresses; the house was given up ; she, Mrs. Hol- royd, was still uncertain what she was going to do.. Then came daily papers, and illustrated weekly, papers, with portraits of the bride and bridegroom, • and I learnt that Una wore the dianmeds 1 had last seen on her mother on that fateful night when she came across the garden to my window with a face like that of a eheetel ghost. It. was all over, and C twain Steyne and his beant fttl mite went away for a honeymoon such as only. those who inherit the earth can hope.for. Amid the, bsauty of nature, and in the cities where music, is, worshipped, and amid all the splendour that the art and culture of the twentieth century can give, these two passed the early months of their married life.

I heard nothing of Mrs. Holroyd, and did not know where to write to her. But at last a letter from Una reached me. It was to beg me to go and see her mother when I Could go to London. "Oh, dear Miss Millet," she said, "I am sit anxicus. Dear little mother has gone to live in the shuts of South Lambeth and nurses the poor. peorle, and does things for the poor children all day long. It is delightful of her, and directly I can get back to town I will go and help her, and 4 look after her; but that is what I am anxious. about. Positively there isn't any":ocly who cares enough to go and look after her a little. Oh, do. please go as soon' as you can." . • Of course I did go as soon as I could, and stepped right into another tragedy, and had to. begin listening again at once. But,l must not tell. about that now. ['Dia EXo].

div.head: PHOTOGRAPHIC NOTES.
div.p: PHOTOGRAPHIC NOTES.
By Veronica.
FLOWER PHOTOGRAPHY_ AND_PELIGION

In le—cturing on the photographing of flowers a m ell- known exhibitor is said to have stated that! before taking up this work be was a convinced atheist, and that as a result of his study cf lioness, be has become a convert to Christianity. COLOUR PHOTOGRAPHY.

The extremely interesting exhibition of The Society of Colour Photographers suggests many thoughts as to the effect that the newer procusses will have upon our I hobby as a whole. Colunr work is evidently going through similar developments to those which were , experienced by photography itself. Just As many early : workers in photography appreciated hard, brilliant con-, tracts, SO the workers in colours, have mostly taken to riotous schemes of red, yellow, blue, green, and orange. The current exhibition shows that many are turning their attention to softer and more delicate subjects, to Indscapes with soft gradations of lieht and shade, and i to subtle harmonies in subject pictures. THEIR EFFECT UPON MONOCHROME WORK. I

I think tbere can be very little doubt that one of the • effects of the study of colours will be an enormous i improvement in the rendering of tones even by those photographers who do not take up colour wcrk. In nearly all photography, there is a heaviness and want of life, light, and gradation, especially in the shadows, which is not at air a necessary result of the photographio methods. It arises from insufficient study of nature,l and can be avoided by proper use of orthochrozuatic methcds, and especially by ample exposure. SHUTTER SPEEDS. Probably many of my readers are just beginning photography, and one of the first things that will trouble them will be exposure, especially if they begin by con- I suiting other =atom's of but small experience, who I will talk as if the difference between one-tenth and one- • fifteenth of a second was a vital matter. Shutter speeds are not strictly comparable with each other, for quite apart from the variation in "efficiency " of different forms of shutter, it is so diffioult to control the exact speeds, and so still more difficult to mark them exactly, that in practice, almost every cheap abutter has a very large percentage of errcit at some, if not all, its speeds. Thereforej your friend's one-fifteenth may be actually a longer exposure than your own one-tenth. AMPLE MARGIN FOR ERROR. While it is quite true that many pictures are over- exposed, and that an immensely larger number are ; under-exposed, the difference of 100 per cent, can be I almost entirely neglected with any ordinary subject and an enormously larger error will, as a general rule, be indicated by the amateur. That is to say, if the correct exposure for a givea subject is one second, it • will not be ruined if it receives only half a second, or if two seconds are given to it. Hence, the differerce between ore-tenth and one-fifteenth, and also the error • in marking of shutter speeds can be completely ignored for all practical pui poses. It is importaidt that beginners should realise the wide margin tbat is allow- able, for ignorance on this point often leads to : bewilderment. Thus, with a subject that requires an ; exposure of one second, a man may give one-sixtieth. He is told by a friend that it is under-exposed, and i probably thinks he is ranking a step in the right direction I by changing his speed to one-fiftieth. While this, of t couree;is a longer exposure than the other, the differ- ; ence is so small that if the under-exposure was serious, ' no improvement will be found in the result. The struggler may give yet another expoinue (say one- I fort:eth) and, still finding the subject hopelessly bad may think that ho has given a wide range of exposure, and begin to attempt to improve upon the result by some other means. THE FIRST LESSON TN EXPOSURE.

It would 1-e a most valuable lesson, and a great saving of time and material,' f every photographer would begin his experience by exposiug a plate in strips with , very widely varied exposures. By polling out the ' slide of the plate-holder half an incb, and making one I exposure, then pelting out another half inch for a ! second exposure, and so on, he may get a very wide range of different exposure effects upon one single ' quarter-plate. He should begin by estimating the real exposure that is necessary PS accurately as he can, and I should then arrange that the middle strip has this exposure, while other strips have many times more and I some have many times less. If the plate is to be -exposed in six strips, and the proper exposure is estimated to be four seconds, it may be well to give exposures consisting of 4,4, 2,2, 1, 1 seconds, / respectively. As the first strip gets all the additional exposure the actual exposure given to the strips will be ` 11, 10, 6,4, 2, and I seconds, respectively. This plate ! should be developed by some one who understands photography, and should well point out which is• actually z hpepirrox .x properly op exposed e cl a strip. a BY RESULTS. If the amateur is in an isolated place where no friend , or dealer can Le relied upon to develop, he should follow the Instructions in his handbook very carefully, and when he thinks the exposure has gone far enough, I should fix and finish his negative, and make a print. I If the development was really complete, he should floc, some detail in all the strips. It may he necessary to give much longer printing to lomestrips than to others, and perhaps the best lesson would be obtained by mak- ing ore print just deep enough to give all the detail that is possible in the under-exposed strips, and another one to bring up all the detail in the over,-exposed portions. It will then be found that in addition to the ever-exposed parts of the negative being dense and slow to print, the contrasts of light and shade will I tend to be slight, whereas the under-exposed portions which print their shadow details very quickly will pro- bably have quite as much density in the highlights as is found in the over-exposed parts. Therefore, the , highlights (sky, etc.) will be bard and white, while the , ehadons are black and without gradation. This : difference, if considered, will help in determining when any subject bus been over-exposed and under-exposed. '

div.head: MOTOR TRAFFIC GRIEVANCES.
div.p: MOTOR TRAFFIC GRIEVANCES.

Letter from Mr. A. J. King, Wilting to a correspondent in the lioutsford Mr. A. J. King, M.P.' refers to the increased motor traffic on the roads, and says : "I think it is clear that the public bare a distinct grievance on necount of the largely inmeased 'motor traffic, and this grievance takes, I think, three torn s—danger to lifeat,cl limb, especially to cbildten and old people ; dust duisance,and tbe rate- payers' grievance owing to the increased cost of upkeep of main roads. Mr. Stranss's 1.111 only deals nith the first of these, end I should like to see in it a clause milking more general a precaution, which is taken now in some parts of Scotland; for regulating the speed of cars when passing a school or church in the main road. To my mind by far the most serious nuisance of nhich the public love the right to complain is the dust nuisance' and hero we are at once met by the mctorist with the reply that this nuisance is caused by the had state of the roads, and that a remedy is to be found in making bettsr roads. . . . I think there can be no doubt that unless motoring in any shape is to be stopped altogether, the remedy runst be found in the different construction of our roads. Whether the roads should continue as now to he a local charge OA tho rates or ehould be taken over by the Government as a national charge is another and a larger question, but I think there is a good deal to be said for the latter prcpc sal."

The Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Company have arranged special through bookings in connection with Anglesey trips on Saturday and Sunday 18th and 15th instant. The Cheshire Lines announce book- ings on Saturday from Central Station, Manchester, at 7.30 a.m., and on Sunday the L. and Y. Rsilway aro running a special train from Rocbdale at G 35 Oldham 7 a.m., and Manchester (Victoria) at 7.30 a.m. The L. and N. W. Successful Event at Warrington.

About 3.000 adults and children assembled on .tne Warrington Football Ground and showed by their hearty end repeated applause, their appreciation of the interesting and varied programme. The girls of Scliffe and St. Ann's again performed some beautiful fiances and great credit if clue to Miss Orton and Miss Rowland for their admirable training.

A spec-ill word of praise is du; to the judges— 'Councillor J. Locker, :qr. 'J. Moore Murray, Mr. T. Pemberton, Mr. 11. Ashton, tr. .1. F. Foster and Mr. A. S. div.head: EDUCATION QUESTION. Position of the Government Bill.
div.p: THE EDUCATION QUESTION. Position of the Government Bill.
INTERVIEW WITH REV. THOMAS LAW.

For some little time past there has been a feeling of uneasiness among Free Churchmen as to the position of the Education Question. Mr. Asquith, in his recent statement in the House, detailed the Government's plans in reference to various measures, but no mention was made of the Education Bill. Consequently there is a feeling of serious unrest as to what is happening or going to happen aa far as education is concerned, and the impression is getting abroad in the country either that education is to be dropped or that there are to be serious concessions. Free Churchmen remember that the Education Question was one of the most prominent issues at the General Election, and are getting to say the least of it, very dissatisfied at the present inaction. 1 In order to ascertain how matters really stand at the present juncture, writes a special correspondent, I waited on the Rev. Thomas Law, the secretary of the National Free Church Council, at his offiee at the Memorial Hall. Mr. Law admitted that he bad received scores of letters complaining of the unsatisfactoriness of the present situation. "I want to assure our Free Church friends "said Mr. Law, " that they need have no fear as to the action of the Government. We are fully assured both by the Prime Minister and the Minister for Education that the Education Bill will be dealt with in the early Autumn. It will, in fact, be one of the principal measures of the Autumn Sessien. It will not be pro- ceeded with before the recess, simply because of the extraordinary pressure of business which must be accomplished before August Ist. But the Rill will be proceeded with as previously introduced. There is no suggestion as to concessions at all, and whatever may happen, at present there are no "Round Table Confer- ences "going on. As a matter of fact, no basis has been found for a Conference, so that the Government will go forward with their measure as it now stands. They fully realise that they are pledged to secure justice, and are in no wise anxious to in the least minimise or postpone the hone.

div.p: WATER POLO.
WARRINGTON v EVERTO'N.

Keen interest was evinced in a Liverpool and Dis- trict League First Division match between Everton and Warrington at Westminster-road Baths, Liverpool on Wednesday, as Everton, mho have an unleaten record, bad to meet a strong team from Warrington. The sides were—Everton : C. Morris (goal), R. J. Skinner (capt.), M. Jones, H. A. Booth, J. F. Winn, T. 0. Cooper, and F. Cleminshaw. Warrington : C. Woods (goal), R. Allen (eapt.), W. Ashton, H. Wolsteu- croft, W. Sutton, S. Walker, and I'. Pemberton. Play was of a fast character, and some good tactics were displayed by both teams. The visitors were the first to score through Ashton, and soon afterwards Booth equalised with a brilliant shot, half-time arriving with the score—Everton I, Warrington I. No more points were notched in the second period, the game ending in a draw.

The Official Receiver said the compapy was a perfectly genuine concern, old establisha, perfectly solvent so far as the tool- making NN, n s concerned, two months ago. div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, July 18, 1908.
OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Latchford Baptist Church.

• At this church on Sunday the anniversary services were held when the preacher, morning arid evening, was the Pastor, the Rev. J. F. Matthews. There were lar,,e attendances, especially in the evening, when the building was crowded andsthe discourses of the rev. gentleman were listened to with great interest. Anthems were creditably rendered by the choir, and Mr. It. E. Burt presided at the organ. An interesting musical service was held in the afternoon, presided over by Mr. James Dodds, who expres.sed the opiidon that Mr. Matthews was worthy of a large church in the town. That was not only his opinion but the opinion of many others, and if it could be arranged he wo:tld be quite willing to subscribe towards the cost. Coyne'llor B Ball gave an interesting address on"Musie and Religion." The soloists were Miss Alice IVoodland (soprano) and Miss Lily Fairbutst (contralto), each of %%Itom was heard to great advantar:e. The collections for the rkty amounted to nearly £l7. ,
Wesleyan Methodist Bible Class League',
Mr. C. E. Parker and Attacks on the alble

The IVesleyan Methodist Bible Class League (Warrington circuit) had arranged to hold an cpea-air meeting at Sankey Bridges on Saturday afternoon but owing to the miserable weather, it had to be abandened. At five o'clock tea was served in the Wesleyan school- room and aftereards a publie meeting was held. Mr. J.C.Holland presided and was supported by the Rev. J.F. Matthews, Mr. C. E. Parker and Mr. hlaile (Latelford). The CII,ITRMAN impressed upon the members of the League the need for greater zeal and deteriuleation in their work, in view of the apathy. indifference and callousness which prevailed. Ile alluded to attacks on the Bible which had recently been made in the town and said one lecturer actually described the Bible as a silly book. They, however, knew what help they had derived by reading the Scriptures and when these attacks' which were as old as the hills, were made they ought to be filled with even greater determination to be loyal to their profession and stick to those truths which were enshrined in the Bible. The great danger of the present age was indifference. The Rev.J.F. Marrrtews said he was glad that Bible Class League had been established and he wished those who had had the framing of the League had allowed their foresight and judgment to have extended a little further and formed a federation of the Bible classes of all the churches in the town. They would then Lave a magnificent fighting force of real twentieth century iron-sides—in feet, a moral, intellectual and spiritual force which would be word to none in any other teen in the kingdom. Bible study should really be the study of all that belonged to their common humanity and should produce in them a catholic sprit, a largejudg- ment, and a tender and sympathetic outlook. Mr. Matthews then proceeded to deal with the qualifications which preachers and teachers should possess and emphasised the necessity of personal fitness, adequate equipment, and efficiency. Mr. C. E. PARKER eaid he could not understand how anyone could call the Bible a silly book. It held sonic of the finest literature, apart altogether from its inspirational character, that there was in existence. It had been aptly described by one writer as the greet Alp of literature; it towered above all other books. From whatever standpoint they judged it, everyone must recogonize that the Bible was a very wonderful book. It had been put into the furnace of criticism again and again, and yet so far as its Teal worth end value was concerned it had come out and there was not even the smell of fire upon it. Then they had in the Bible some of the finest poetry in literature. Some one spoke of the Bible having ransacked creation to lay its ' treasures on Jehovah's sitar. ILe book which con- tained the writings of such a men as Paul, and literature covering such a vast period, could not in any sense be called a silly book. At the same time he felt that there were some points of criticism to which the defenders of the Bible were open. He had heard it said that the BiLle had been the greatest impediment to human progress, that there had scarcely been a wrong which men had set themselves to right, but the defenders of that wrong had gone to the Bible for its defence. There was no doubt a great deal of truth in that criticism as was instanced by the arguments against the abolition of slavery, temperance work and other forward movements, which were drawn from the Bible. The great mistake in regard to the treatment of the Bible by its defenders was that they had used it in a way in which God never intended it to be used. The Bible , was not given to us to teach us astronomy, geology and science. Those were things that God in His wisdom gave us brains and knowledge to find out for ourselves, an H d is spirit, just as It inspired men of old to write what was in the Bible, had led men into the truth in other wiles apart altogether from the Bible. If they pit the Bible in its right place they would treat it not as a scientific but as a great moral and spiritual book. The great key note of the Bible was contained in the first four words: "In the beginning God," and it was the book from which all got to know the great deep truths of our life. 'I be Cross of Christ and the lesson of love and sacrifice that it taught was the thing the world needed most and was the only thing that would remove the sin and sorrow of mankind.
Representatives of the various Bible classes having presented worts cn their work the meeting closed.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRA.GEDIES.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRA.GEDIES.
MELANCHOLIA LEADS TO SUICIDE.

Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest at the Warrington Police Station on Thursday evening, touching the death of Eliza Underhill, aged 71 Tears, 10, Frederick-street, Warrington. Thomas Underhill, contractor (who has been on a visit here from New York), son of the deceased, said his mother was the widow 'of the late William Underhill, who visa a sub-contractor. At 4.20 on Wednesday afternoon she was in the kitchen with witness and his wife, he being engaged in writing a letter. Deceased went into the parlour, shutting the door behind her. After an absence of about two minutes the returned to the kitchen and it was seen that her throat was cut and bleeding profusely. Witness laid her on the stairs and called in Dr. Jago, who said life was extinct. The razor with which the act was committed was witness's pro- perty. It was kept at the back of the top shelf of the cupboard, out, it was supposed, of the way of the deceased.

------. To answer to the Coroner witncrs said he bad been staying with his mother for three weeks. She had teen strange in her manner, and particularly so on Wednes- day. They had been cautioned by a medical man that she might attempt to do away with herself. Dr. Ferguson said he was called to see Mrs. Under- hill when she first came to Warrington and found her suffering from a tendency to melancholia. She had delusions and particularly the idea that her people wanted to send her nutty. Witness had been asked to give evidence in case it might be thought that the family bad not done everything that they could for her. Witness knew that they had done. When he last saw deceased in April, her mental condition appeared to be much better.
A verdict of "Suicide during temporary insanity " was returned.
CHILD'S SAD END.

Mr. Brighouse then held an inquiry into the circum- stances attending the death of Rose Damll, the two- year-old child of Thomas liaseall, green grocer, 174, Lovely-lane; who sustained fatal burns on Monday. Deceased's father stated that he was present at the Infirmary when in arid died at 11-5- urrTuttduTnlght i . Ills %ire, n trying to save-the deceased, had Ler hands very Ladly burned end was not able to attend the inquest. She had told witness that at 12.20 (noon) on Monday she heard screaming and on running into the yard found deceased with her clothing on fire. She ran to her and tried to put out the flames and called for assistance. Councillor Dickenson, who happened to he near, came to her aid. She could not say how the child got on fire. There was some burning straw in a shed in the yard but whether deceased or some-one else had set it on fire they did not know. - Councillor James Dickenson, 53, Froghall-lane, said be was in the neighbourhood of Lovely-lane and heard the screams. On turning round he saw the deceased's mother with the child in her arms. Witness ran to her, took off his coat and wrapped it round the child who was then conveyed to the Infirmary. The mother was severely burned about the hinds. The coroner: It seems to he ?lather a mystery how the child got on fire. Councillor Dickenson said he did not go into the yard as he was too much occupied in attending to the

-.Te-r.geant Stuart said that how, the straw became ignited was a mystery. There was no onerbut tlio child about. Dec(ased had been accustomed to playing with match stalks but not with matches,andsbe ‘ras afraid of fire. The jury returned a Terdict of "Accidental death," the Coroner remarking that evidently the child had got hold of a match.
