div.head: [ALL lITGIITS BEsEnvift.]
div.p: [ALL lITGIITS BEsEnvift.]
JACKS RIDE TO MILLIE
BY B. L FARJEON,
Author of "The Sacred Nugget," "The King of Noland," "Aaron the Jew," "The House of White Shadows," "A Szeret Inheritance," &c.

Never in his life had Jack Marlowe been so long over his toilet es he -vas on this 19th day of December. It was in the early years of the discovery of gold in Australia, and Jack had been one of the pioneers on the track of gold in the gullies aid on the hills. White buckskin riding-pants, with leather belt round the waist (braces on Kangaroo Fiat and on all the gold- fields were looked ullion as effeminate), anti over the belt a broad red silk sash with fringes ; a striped white and blue linen shirt open at the neck ; and a Panama hat so fine and light and thin that it would have cxeited the envy of Bond- street dandies, who in these more modern years affect this fashion of head-gear. These few items completed his attire, and quite enough they were OH this blazing hot day, when the temperature, before the sun reached its meridian, was likely to make a record. But Jack didn't care. Not a bit. Nor would he have cared had he been going out into a heavy snowstorm. What matters the weather to a man over head and cars in love? As Jack was. And the girl, whose bright eyet and winsome face had worked this marvel in him, was as much in love as he. She was waiting for him in her father's canvas tent in the Omeo district, a hundred and thirty miles from Kangaroo Flat, and knew that on this day her lover would be riding her way, and that when he arrived he might ask her a certain supreme question for which she had her answer ready. Curious was it not, that loving each other as they did, this question had not yet been asked? There was a reason for it. Long as Jack had been on the goldfields, 'following each new rush, and working manfully from sunrise to sundown, fortune had not smiled upon him—until lately. To be precise, until just two months ago, • when Jack, having purchased for a song a quarter share in a claim on a quartz reef for which the men had been digging for over a year, received his reward. At a hundred and forty odd down in the bowels of the earth the golden reef was struck. How many or how few ounces of gold to the ton of quartz would be the result, had yet to be ascer- tained, but there were specks of gold in the stone, and pretty freely distributed, and every du a nice-looking specimen of gold and quarts , revealed itself to the delighted eyes of the owners of the claim. The prospect, therefore, was good, and the men calculated that the first crushing would go at least two or three ounces to the ton. When they came upon it the reef was very thin, not more than two or three inches; but it was widening out, and stone began to come up freely. Of course, the first thing Jack Marlowe did, upon the advent of this stroke of luck, was to write 'to Millicent (Milly for short) and tell her about it, and she wrote back and said how glad she was; and although the letters were not open loves letters there must have been a lot of lows hidden somewhere in the words that were written, else why should both Milly and Jack put their letters under their pillows when they went to bed, having previously drawn much sweet- ness from the inanimate paper with their lips ? Then followed another letter from Jack. They had had a crushing of thirty tons, and the yield was a cake. of gold weighing two hundrod and eighty ounces, Which, after the payment of expenses, put over two hundred pounds into Jack's pocket for his quarter share. Then another crushing, and another sum of two hundred and fifty pounds into the happy IIIRD•6 pocket. Following this, a third letter from Jack, saying that he was coming to the Oineo to spend Christmas with Milly and her father, and would start from Kangaroo Flat on December 19th, which would make him due on the 22nd. - _ -

"I've bought a horse," wrote Jack—"a beauty. A bay it is, and the gentlest creature! And I've had 'M' engraved on the harness. That is why. I am coming down in the saddle instead of by Cobb's coach. And I am bringing Ponto with me. Perhaps when you see him— But never mind," &c., &c. Ponto was a splendid greyhound, of which faithful, handsome animal Alllly had expressed the greatest admiration on a previous visit which Jack had paid her father. The refer.. ence to itt. on the harness !dilly perfectly under. stood, and it set her heart beating faster; but why Jack should say, referring to Ponto: "Perhaps—hut never mind," was too veiled and mysterious for understanding. Still, she was satisfied that it meant somethinr, delightful, fox what did Jack do that was not delightful ?

• - Trat these two young people should write to each other, and should commence their letters with "My dear and "My dear Jack," without being engaged, needs explanation. They were friends and chums, as little boy and girl, in the old country. When Milly was fifteen her father with his family emigrated to Australia. Jack was already there. A couple of years ago Jack heard of her being in the Omeo district. HI wrote to her, taking the post-office as an address. She received the letter and replied to it. He went to see his old friends—a walk of a hundred and,thirty• miles is nothing to a gold- digger. There's no •telling what kind of good fortune one might meet with on the road, perhaps a big • nugget sticking out of the earth (such things have been, and the discovery of a new goldfield. And when a pretty.girl—a sweetheart of childhood who gave the promise of growing into a beautiful woman—is in question, what shall stop the pulsing of hot young blood? And' let me tell you, woman was worth more than her weight in gold in those days. She ruled the roast,' was queen of all she surveyed; the plainest 'of them had a hundred suitors, and could pick and choose. ' So now you know why Jack Marlowe took so long over his toilet on the morning of that 19th day of December. He was going to Milly, with a hope in his heart which made it a very garden of joy. A manly young fellow, five feet eleven in his stockinged feet, strong, litho, clear-skinned, much browned by the sun just now; curly hair, brown beard, which he did not allow to grow too long, willing heart, willing hand—precisely the kind of man to win a girl's heart and to win his way in the world: -Barring the costume he might have' stood as a model for a brave Soldier in the days of old Greece. It was the free life on the. goldfields,- the working in fresh air, the indepen- dent spirit that such a life brings to a man that had raade._hina—what be was.. Compare such a man—there were thousands of them—with the humdrum worker in a crowded city. No, don't compare them, it would make you sad. Outside his tent he was accosted by a mate or two, who had an inkling of the errand he was • going on. "Good luck, Jac7k," they said. "Thank you, mates," said he. "The same to you." Mounted on his bay horse he commenced his journey to the Omeo. NOW, he could have done the hundred and thirty•miles in less than three days had he been so minded, for the bush roads- are soft to a ' horse's feet, and sixty-five miles a day in the saddle was thought little of. But he would not overwork the bay. He wanted it to be quite fresh and light-hearted, as ha himself was, when he drew rein at the door of- the canvas tent in which Milly lived. So he settled to de forty-five miles the first day, forty-five -miles the second, forty the third. A blue blanket was neatly disposed on the front of the saddle, and he had sufficient food for the three days, for he intended to sleep in the bush, which in such weather a man might Jo without danger of catching &lid or getting the ague. He had a Colt's revolver -at the back of his belt beneath the red silk each, and a fossicking knife beside it. Disposed about the saddle were an axe' hobbles and bell for his nag, and fodder also; afrying-pan to fry his chops in, a packet of tea, and a tin pannikin. In his breast pocket were his cutty pipe, a couple of cakes of cavendish„ and .a couple of boxes of matches. Some other trifles also such as a gold watch • and chain for Milly, and 's bracelet for aid two or three specimens from the • golden rtef for Milly, and—yes, a wedding-ring for •Milly; and all these trifles were nestled in soft white wool, as such trifles should be. And there was something more precious than all these —Milly's portraitsin a ease, which he took out I don't know how many times an hoar to look at and kiss.

So he rode on, iv happy man if ever man was, and on the first day he did his forty-fire miles, put the hobbles on his horse and the bell round her neck, having first taken her—a mare she was— to a creek in which there was still a little water left. Then he let her loose. ronto nact runnier, along at his side the whole of the day in great aajoyment of the outing, and now, having slaked

- his thirst, sat with his paws stretched Wan-etch- ing his master frying his chops over the camp fire. He knew that he would have his share. After supper Jack and Ponto had a chat, and Jack skewed his dog Milly's picture, and asked him what he thought of it, and I daresay talked a lot of nonsense, to which Ponto had not the slightest objection. Then the two drew away from the camp Ere and slept beneath a glorious panoply of stars. I need not tell you who played the principal part' in Jack's dreams. Ponto's ;dreams I know nothing whatever about. They wele all on the road again early on the mornin r of the second day, which was much more enjoyable than the first for was not jack drawing nearer and nearer to Milly? And visions ol the future rose before him, and ho sang to the trees of eilver hark. It was terribly hot "About a hundred and twenty in the shade, - Panto," said Jack, and Ponto waggled his great tail, as mueli as to say:, "What does that matter ? We're getting nearer and nearer to I think I out to say atword about Ponto's ”llar. It Vas a new collar, and On the silver ok.t I was 'engraved the name of 11E11y—only her ChristNn name, mi.! d. And beneath the name the words, in very small letters, "Will you ?" Rather enigmatical, is it not ? When night fell the second forty-five miles were done, and they supped and slept as on the first night, and rose ,on the third morning—that is, Jack did—not a bit the worse for the blazing sun, which eeemed to promise something even more scorching than on the previews two days. Before he went to sleep on this second night Jack discovered ttat hc hi alse!_e a misealeula- tion as to the commissariat The food that he thought would have been sufficient for three day, was enough only for two, and on the third rimm- ing they had short commons at breakfast. Thie did not trouble him mucha-for he had but forty miles to go before things would be set right: He knew the road pretty well, though the greater part of it lay through the bush, chiefly cattle tracks. A little way on the road he met a shepherd who, hearing whither he was bound, informed him that by taking a sheep track whick lay - off the wider traeks over which he hai travelled he could save a good eight miles. He accepted the information gleefully. Eight miler saved! That meant an hour nearer to his dem Milly. The shepherd pointed out the narrow track and gave him directions, and they bade each good•day. Off he set on the shorter route, and cantered gently on, followed contentedly by Ponto. His thoughts were on the dear girl he hoped to wed, and this probably, and perhaps ; some over-confidence in himself, made him more careless than be should have . been. At about • eleven o'clock ho suddenly became aware that lie had lost the track that had been pointed out tc him, and that the weeds through which he was riding had become thicker. ,Dismounting, he looked keenly in every direction for . the track, ' but could not find it. The forest in which he, found himself was trackless. He had no fear, however; his compass would guide him. Putting his hand into his pocket for it he found that it was gone. He remembered taking it out last night, and he supposed he must have put it on the ground and forgotten to take it up again. Very careless of him, but he did not doubt that he would soon light upon the track again. Mounting his horse he proceeded at a walking pace, bending over the saddle and examining every inch of the ground with keen and anxious eyes. The annoyance was that it would be late before reaching Milly. And there she was, in his mind's eye, standing at the door, ;looking out for him. Too bad to'keep her waiting, and a piece of real hard luck for himself. No trace of the track met his gaze,and,iudeed, he soon had the sense to acknowledge that no shepherd would drive his sheep through such a forest of trees. Thicker and thicker they grew, silverbark, iron-bark, gum, in thousands of ; thousands upon thousands. He could hardly see ; the white, heat-laden clouds that lay like the ; spell of doom above them. No sign there to guide him. His compass gone, he did not know whether he was wending north, south, east, or . west Then he tried to retrace the way he had come, but he only grew more bewildered. 10 was trapped in a trackless forest To the right or to the left, backward or forward, it was all the same. Dismounting again he marked with his knife Mille of the trees so that he might recognise them if in his efforts to escape he came upon them, and then turned in the opposite direction. But to .go straight through the laby- rinth was impossible, and soon he could not determine whether he was going in an opposite direction, and an hour afterwards he was con- founded by coming upon the trees he had , marked. He must have been travelling in a circle. ,He looked at his watch. It was noon. And Milly was waiting for him! In all this immense forest there was not .a bird, and there was no sound or movement except that of his feet eranchiug the parched leaves with which the earth was thickly carpeted. The silence So weighed upon him that he started singing, but soon broke down. The sense of impending-calamity stole upon him. There were many records of men, trapped as lie was trapped, whose whitening bones, discovered after weeks or manths had elapsed, denoted the agonising fate that—had befallen them. But away with these forebodings! A nice kind of courage to shew when Milly was waiting for him "Horses have more sense than men," thought he, and he mounted into the saddle and sat there with idle hands. The horse took a few steps, then stopped dead. "Can yoa do anything, Ponto ?" he asked. The dog looked up with mournful eyes. - But Jack went on and on, praying for a sign. None came. ; His watch marked one o'clock— two o'clock—three o'clock. He led his horse now, this way and that, and looked, and listened, and prayed. But the horrible monotony of these myriad trees was maddening, and he kept closing his eyes to shut out the view.- He had not a drop of water to drink, and he could find no creek or water-course to afford relief. His horse —Milly's horse—nosed every inch of ground for Moisture. Ponto's tongue was hanging out of his mouth. In those regions there is no twilight. Suddenly darkness fell upon him. It was night. "Good Heavens!" he groaned. "Milly is waiting for inn!" He threw himself upon the crackling leaves, and, happily or unhappily, the mercy of forget- fulness was granted to him. - I think he courted it, hoping that sleep would strengthen him. ; When he awoke in the morning he was seized with despair. His horse was gone. Ponto was gone. And the white, blinding clouds heralded another day of maddening heat. - He got to his feet and wandered aitnlessly this way alai that, with a torturing thirst upon him. ; His tongue chive to the roof of his mouth. But worse than this was the thought of Milly. Vhat construction would she place upon his ' absence? That he had been fooling her? Shudders ran through him. He felt that he was , lost, and that he would leave a shameful memory ; behind him. .

..... _ The day passed without a sign, and night fell again. "Perhaps this is death," he thought, u a stupor stole upon him, and all things faded from his sight. "Are I still alive ?" was the mute question in his mind as he opened his eyes in the early riiorning. Yes, he WaS still alive, and, thank Heaven! he had not yet gone mad. He had in his pocket a little book with some blank leaves in it. He took it Out, and with feeble fingers commeneed a letter to Milly. "Dear, darling !dilly,— I die loving you. I have loved you all niy life." But when he had scrawled these words he lifted himself up. He would not die—be would not, he would not! There must- be a way—there must be a road out ef.this dead, eternal stilhiesi! Yes, there was— there, in the distance, the goldfield of the Omeo. He saw it, saw the white tents of the diggers; saw the men at the windlasses, saw them stoop- ing over the creek—the blessed creek with water in it—saw the picks at work, and the diggers signalling to each other. One was standing on the top of a great mound of pipeclay, beckoning to him. "Come along, Jack, come along!" "I am coming, I am coming!" he cried, with joy. ! ! And then, as he staggered towards the man on the pipeclay mound, he began to sing in a cracked, dry undertone, "For Bonnie Annie Laurie.", It was Milly'a favourite song. But !as he stumbled forward the man faded, the white tents, the miners at the windlasses, the blessed creel: of water, all, all melted away! It was a v!sion he had seen. No objects met his sight exeept the horrible trees, staring down upon him and mocking him. 'Yes, mocking him! He ! saw the fiendish glare in their eyes; he saw their ! s-inning faces. "Well, let me die he mutely implored. "But show me first where I can get 0 ,rink of water. Then kill me!" The wean) silence answered him. No other answer. crniy that. And the sun—the hot, blistering sun! How cruel, how merciless! "Dear Lord in [leaven!" he prayed. "Take the sun in, and send the rain! aguzo me with it, drown me is
It—but send, oh! send it—send the blessed rain!" Then he sank to the ground—to die!

He awoke—where—how? Was it Milly who was clasping him to her breast ? Had she come to him in the spirit world ? And had his horse come toe? And rout° ? "Milly!" he muttered. - "Yes, Tack!" she answered, moistening his lips with water. "Are we in Heaven, Mil.ly ?" "I am Jack." _ _
"How did you come ?' ."Ponto led mo here, Jack. He came to tho tent and dragged at my frock, and 1 followed him. Thank Heaven-0, thai:k Heaven 1 fol- lowed him t"
"You read what was on his collar' Milly ?" "Yes, Jack. Do you feel better, Jack ?" well—quite well." De bhifted his position, SO that his arms were round her. "I don't believe I am dead."

There was a long, delicious pause, and a prayer of thankfulness in both their -heart& Then: "Milly, will you ? " "Will I what, Jack ' "Have me? "Why, you've got me, Jack!" It was a fact, for he was clapping her close. "You darling!" be muttered. "You darling— you darling !
[TnE Esp.]

div.head: WIRRAL SHOW.
div.p: WIRRAL SHOW.
The King Wins Three Prizes.

For many years it has been the custom to look for rain on the occasion of the Wirral Agricultural Show, but Wednesday falsified anticipations, the day being bright and fine for the sixty-sixth annual show. In other respects, too, the opening differed from that of precious yearn, having a record number of entries, viz., 4,460, and numbering among the exhibitors his Majesty the King. Of the total exhibits, the leading class numerically was the dog section, with 1,288 entries. Pigeons came next, with 988, and poultry following third with 893 exhibits. Horses numbered 450, cattle 139. pigs 52, sheep 31, cheese 85, butter and eggs 63, while rabbits and cavies numbered well, as did stand exhibits, The ground at Bebington is ideally equipped for show purposes, and nowhere wns there any evidence of overcrowding, while nowhere did any of the sections seem to straggle apart from the main displays. The show is one that has always commanded the patronage of notable persons in North and West Cheshire and South-West Lancashire. The King's exhibits, of course, provoked more interest than those of any other individual, and it rive widespread satis- faction when it became known 'that His Majesty had proved successful in each of his entries. The Duke of Eutherlsnd had two exhibits in the sheep class, sent from his Lillesball home farm. One being a shearling ram which carried off the first prize in its own class, and also won the 'S Edmund Taylor " challenge bowl, valued twenty-five guineas, given for tho hest exhibit of Shropshire sheep in the show exhibited tly a member of the Wirral and Birkenhead Agricultural Society. His Grace's other exhibit, three shearling ewes, secured a second prize in its class. The Duke also exhibited in the horse class. taking a second prize for a Shire filly, foaled in 1907, vr ith his bay filly, `• Lilleshall Countess," and a first with a Shire mare, any age, with foal at foot. His Grace the Duke of Westminster exhibited in the cattle section without SIMMS' but was compensated by a number of successes in tho horse ring, including a trot with his bay Shire filly "Phenol." Of the 450 horses shown the majority wike in the "light" classes, some of which have yet to be judged. Taken throughout the horses were above the average in quality. This was specially noted in the oar-horse section. Notwithstanding the increasing use ahnotor traction in the larger industrial towns, the demand for draught horses shows no falling off, and thanks to the encouragement which breeders are receiving nlihe from landlords and from the buyers of big-boned animals, Lancashire and Cheshire are becoming more and more famed for the excellence of their shires. The cattle were good, and that apart from the fart that the King bad sent of his best. His Majesty's exhibitsareswo bulls and a heifer from the farm at Windsor. The roan Eynndel took a first" in the open competition for bulls calved in 1906 and the Miller challenge cup for the best shorthorn bull in the show. Another entry, Royal Windsor (shown at the Royal Show), "calved in or before 1905," took first prize in its class; and among the shorthorn heifers calved in 1906 the King's Marjorie, a particularly fine beast, took a " first " and the Honk challenge cup for the best, shoithorn cow or heifer in the yard. Other successes with shorthorns were gained by Mr. Miller, of Birkenhead: Mr. Cornelius, of Eastham ; and Mr. Proctor, of Mobberley. In the four classes for dairy cows, Mr. Tom Hunter, of Lancaster; Mr, S. S. Raingill, of Altrincham; Mr. J. H. Maden, of Bacup ; and Mr. W. Ford, of Sandbacb, were to the fore. Apart from these the dairy cattle generally were only moderate. The explsnation offered is that farmers cannot Afford to sacrifice their best milking stock to show purposes and are content when Once they have secured a good strain. The Channel Islands end Kerry cattle were few in number but a creditable group. In the Channel Islands section Mr. J. de Knoop, of Tarporley, carried everything before him. A visit to the cheese shed served as a corrective to the widely accepted theory that Cheshire is the last place in which to expect to find a perfect cheese. Not only were the entries numerous but competition was the keenest. The Joseph Houk challenge bowl was taken by Miss Alice Holley, of Nnutwich, and the Butler challenge bowl by Mr. John Di I worth,of Marley. In contrast with cheese, batter was disappointing, at all events from the Cheshire point of view, for Southern competitors triumphed in the classes of most account. The W. H. Lever challenge bowl was awarded to Mrs. hlildon, of Morchard Bishop, Devon, a competitor whose name is known thoughout the country; but the North secured one of the first prizes through Mre. G. B. Robinson, of Nantwich, and ihns hada some amends for the success of a second Devon competitor, Mrs. Bern of Cove.

The President for the year is Sir Gilbert Greenell, Mr. Joseph Hap, of Birkenhead, chaitman of the council. and Mr. T. Davier, of Bebington, vice-chair- man. Mr. A. H. Edwardson- is secretary, and for the first time the show was held as one of the Federation of Lancashire and Cheshire Agricultural Societies. The judges were.—Pigs: Colonel F. A. Walker- Jones, Burton, Westmorland. Sheep : Shropshires or any other Downs, Mr. John Smith, %Volga!! ; any long- woolled variety, Mr. J. R. Kirkham, Gosforth, Lacis. Cattle: Shorthorns, Mr. W. Bateman, Halton,Lancaster; dairy cows, Mr. G. B. Nelson,. Gorstoug ; Choitnel Islands and Kerry, Mr. G. P. Mead, Shrensbury. Horses: Shires, Mr. John Blundell, Scotforth, Lan- caster ; Mr. A. E. Freshney, Manhy, Louth ; and Mr. Edward Whittaker, Blackpool ; hunters, Mr. Walter C. Tinsley, Ashbourne •, leapers, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart. ; Mr. T. Lousdale, Hooton ; and Mr. Walter C. Tinsley, Ashbourne • hackneys. saddle and harness, Mr. C. E. E. Cooke, Baidock, Herts. Cheese: Mr. W. W. Gunstone, Sheffield • and Mr. R. Hancock, Manchester, Butter : Miss Chridopherson, Hooton ; and Miss A. M. Harrison, Warrington. Among the prize-wieners were the following - - : CATTLE.

"Four years ago eczema broke cat on my hands and arms and I became so had that I was un- able even to dress my- self and I dared not put my hands in water. Of course I went to see a doctor, but he held out very slight hope of re- covery. I persevered ,with the treatment he recommended, but • without any good re- sult. At last I called on another doc- tor, but he failed also to bring me any benefit. I was suffering terribly then, and I thought I should go out of my mind, as I could neither sleep nor rest, night or day. The skin was all hanging in ribbons, and the arms looked just like raw beefsteak, while the irritation was so terrible that I got desperate sometimes and felt I would like to scratch my arms to pieces. I went to three other doctors, and then I attended the - Hospital, but no one seemed to be able to conquer the disease, and I was on the very brink of despair when I was advised by the matron of another hospital to give Cuticura Remedies a trial. I put some Cuticura Ointment on the sores, and then I had the best night's rc.st I had had for many a long day. I continued the applications and also used Cuticura Soap and Cuticura Resolvent Pills. I seemed to improve all the time, and before I had used up one box of Cuticura Ointment I could do things in the house which I had not been able to do for four years. By the time two boxes of Cuticura Ointment bad been used I was completely cured and my arms and hands, which had been all laceration and blood, were cov- ered •by a beautiful new skin. Now they are in as sound condition as over. I have paid pounds upon pounds for doc- toring all for nothing, and now I can say the Cuticura Remedies are worth their weight in gold. The Borough Member made CROSFIELD AND his third speech in the -xnE PosTmEig. House of Commons on Thursday, and once again showed himself to he fully alive to the necessities of the occasion and mindful of his constituents' interests. His "maiden" speech, delivered just over a year ago, supported the declaration of the late Premier—that "the will of the people shall Prevail" in curtailing the powers of veto exercised by the House of Lords. Only a few weeks ago Mr. Crosfield defended Warrington's position in respect of the Liverpool Corporation Water Bill, cznd his protest, added to the endeavours of our own Corporation, resulted in a clause being added to the 'Bill which preserved Warrington's right to Vyrnwy water if required. On Thursday, Mr. Crosfield championed the cause • of the postmen, and Warrington postmen in Particular, after following an animated debate for fnor hours before his opportunity came. The 3lember's point was in respect of the new classifi- Ration scheme introduced by the Postmaster .General, which places the wages of postmen who )in the service at a future date on a different • basis from that which has previously existed. In Warrington it would mean a' reduction to a minimum of 17s. and a maximum of -2•51., and Mr. Crosfield pointed out that the former would be less than the local labouring wage, and the latter little more than was • Paid to builders' labourers. He urged a reconsideration of the matter, and the Post- ' /fluter General promised that he would be prepared to consider the case of indi- vidual districts. We have reason to believe that Crosfield'a intervention will bear good fruit, nod that Warrington may be one of the individual ti districts which shall not suffer by the classification scheme. In any case, local post-office officials owe the Borough Member their hearty thanks—which they will have an opportunity of tendering next "Thursday. Under the circumstances just com- mented upon it is an interesting coincidence that On Thursday the Postralster Gsneral will open the new post office at Warrington, and be the guest of the Borough Member here afterwards. The entente cordiale between the Member and the Alinister should then be further cemented and the Postmen's prospects correspondingly improved.

div.head: POLITICS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: THE POLITICS OF THE WEEK.

EBY OUR LONDON CORREPONDENT.] • There is a great rush in Parliamentary politics now, as only a fortnight, after this week is out, remains for the winding up of business before the holidlys, which members of Parliament certainly require to prepare them for renewed work in an autumn sitting already fixed to begin on Octeber 12th. MR. ASQUITH'S MANAGEMENT.

_ It is noticeable that ia the Prime Minister's plans for expediting the work of Parliament in these two weeks, nothing is sacrificed of Ministerial intentions. The time-honoured " massacre of the innocents " has no place in his scheme. He has not brought in Bills to abandon them. If there is anything in the way of slaughtering to be done, the House of Lords is left to perform this unenviable task. It is astonishing to find the "Spectator " laying it'down that " coma tempered by fits' is apparently the Ministerial idea as regards legislation," and that waste of the early part of the session is the cause of hurry-scurry and late hours at the close. This might have been a good description of previous Parliaments but the distinguishing feature of the present one, and particu- larly daring this session, has been that the time devoted to Ministerial measures has been carefully mapped out from tho very beginning. Where, suspension of the rule closing sittings at eleven was necessary to get Bills through, it was moved even in the early days. The Whips ought to have their due share of credit, and in this connection the popularity of the new Chief Whip, Mr. "Jack" Pease, must be noted. The political news of the week includes the report of a dinner given to him at which he told some excellent stories of Parliamentary life. THE WHIP'S REMINISCENCES. One of Mr. Pease'e tales is timely, seeing that members are now being called on to sit half through the night to push business through. On one occasion a member, who was sitting at the table at which Mr. Pease told the story, went home at seven o'clock in the morning expecting to find his wife full of sympathy for him after his sacrifice of a night's rest at the altar of duty. To his surprise sho received him with scorn and indignation, and at last met his attempts at explanation with a round accusation of lying. In her own justification she produced a telegram from Mr. Pease urging him to come down and relieve his fellowlegislators who had been sitting up all night The explanation was that the Whip had failed to's notice the member's attendance, and for this he wa not entirely to blame. The sacrifice of the bon. member had not been so complete as it seemed. He had it kept himself under the eyes of the Whips, but bad spend the intervals between divisions in cosy corners of -the House enjoying furtive naps. No doubt Mr. Pease nobly played hi a part in the work of domestic reconciliation. CARRYING OVER. Time and daylight saving expedients are now in fashion, and there seems to be coming into practical politics a suggestion long obvious, but hitherto unavailing against the conservative tendencies of Parliament. 1t is that Bills not finished in one session should not die a natural death, but be carried on into the next. This would be a great boon to private members as well as to the Government. The Access to Mountains Bill, a measure of Mr. Trevelyan's, has , occupied five or six sittings of a Standing Committee this session. Suddenly it has had to be dropped, because there is no chance now of a private member's Bill passing. It seems a pity that the five or six days' labour in Committee should be lost. The Marquis of Lansdowne supported the idea of ,` carrying over," which had originally been mooted by Mr. Asquith. The readiness of the Opposition to encourage this time- and measure-saving scheme seems to have led to reflection on the part of the Earl of Crewe, the new Liberal leader in the Lords, who has now euggestod the wisdom of consideration and caution against carrying this reform too far. Wisely so; for no one knows what unforeseen dangers lurk in constitutional innovations, (specially when they are welcomed by the enemy. Still, for the better organization of Parliamentary business, and in order to deprive the House of Lords of an excuse for rejecting Bills on the plea of want of time to consider them, some such expedient as " carrying over" must sooner or later be adopted. -- • ----
The Examiner, Saturday, July 18, 1908.

div.head: SCANDAL IN THE NAVY.
div.p: SCANDAL IN THE NAVY.

Somewhat - tedious discussions in Committee of Supply on the Navy Estimates this week have been relieved by the intrusion of a topic which has been more keenly discussed in the tea and smoke rooms than in the House' namely, the supposed strained relations between Lord Charles Beiesforcl and Sir John Fisher, and also between Lord Charles and Sir Percy Scott. The rules of the House have prevented any but the most guarded discussion of this exciting bit of gossip ; but the good feeling of the House and the discretion of Ministers, and also of ex-Ministers, have limited the public allusions to what would be a painful scandal, if it is true. Ministers have wisely treated the story of dissensions in high places in the Navy as "unverified rumours" and so have given the persons involved an opportunity of compos- ing their differences, and averting the serious consequences to the individuals concerned. The debates on the Navy by the experts leave on the public mind a confused impression, but allusions to personal differences on the other hand produce a clear and emphatic conviction that this is a cause of inefficiency that cannot and will not be tolerated. There is nothing the nation is so proud of as the personnel of the Navy. It counts for more than even the ships._ The public will not have rot setting in there on any account. THE BUDGET BILL.

At last the Finance Bill, as the Budget is called when it gets into statutory form, is getting through its final stages. The debates have turned mainly on tea, sugar, and income tax. There is a Food deal of regrettable bitterness on the part of the Labour Party in these debates which are led by Mr. Snowden, the financial authority in that party. He is an able man who would go much further if he were less aggressive. lie is in danger of ruffling the smooth and conciliatory disposition of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. There is a failure to recognise how great have been the achievements of the Government for the betterment of Labour this Session, achievements with which the Labour Party would otherwise have every right to associate themselves. The impression is being pro- duced that, in order to claim more than their share of credit, the Labour party are imperilling the good work that the Liberal party are doing. If the House of Lords should be so ill-advised as to accept the "Spectator's" advice to postpone the Old Age Pensions Dill, it is certain that the Labour Party will have to share the responsibility of this postponement of the hopes of the Aged Poor, because it is on utter- ances of the Labour Party that the Lords will ' certainly rely for their attempted justification. A LESSON IN TAItIFP REFORM.

The cause of Free Trade has been greatly served by the foolish ardour of those Tariff Reformers who tried to make a case for the hop-growers, with the result that a House of Commons Committee, presided over by an acute mind like that of Sir William J. Collins, has made a searching investigation into the whole state of their industry. The masterly report just issued proves that to put an import duty on hops with the idea of saving the home industry from the inroads of the foreigner, and of punishing the foreign competitor, would not only be useless, but very harm- ful to this country. The importation of hops is shown to have little to do with the depressed state of the hop- growing business. The main factor in the case is the introduction of the cold-storage system, by which the excess of hops in one year can be held over to make up for another year's scarcity. The import duty would not help the bop-grower even at 40s. It would have to be much bigger to be effective. And even at that figure it goes far beyond the small duty which the Tariff Reformers have held to be all that is necessary. It would not be a ten per cent, but a ' 40 per cent. duty; it would be a tax on the raw material of an important industry; it would handicap our own brewers; and the burden, instead of being paid by the foreigner, would ultimately (and in fact almost immediately) he passed on to the public, who in the end must always pay for these tariff reform experiments. lIOP

--,-- 11-I,at is worth further investigation in regard to the hop duty agitation is the history of the " dumping" of hops from America. Everybody must remember tha great fuss made about the shipment of Canadian Pacific hops to this country a few months ago, and how question after question was asked in Parliament about it. There was a great outcry about the ruin of a British industry, and the zealous Sir Gilbert Parker made the rafters of the House of Commons ring with his strenuous agitation on the subject at question-time. It appears that the shipment was "chiefly old hops." and it is alleged that these hops have been 'dumped' here with the hope of securing such advantage as

might accrue to the vendor in the event of a duty of 40s. a cwt. being imposed in accordance 'with the suggestion made by many xvitnesses." The inference htre is that dumping—in this case, at all events—is not a result of free trade but of speculation in Tariff Reform. If the suggestion is correct, it shows that some clever engineers have been hoist with their own petard. Also that the fears of those- who have said that a tariff would lead to endless intriguing in the lobbies of Patliament and to the corruption of English politics are well justified. I TIM TRUE MEASURES OF RELIEF. The Committee among their suggestions include not only the marking of foreign hops so long as English ones have to be marked, but also the marking if possible, of beer bottles and barrels with the amount of foreign hop contents. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. Let the proof of the beer be in the drinking ; and let the consumer decide for himself whether he will have the foreign beer or not. The prohibition of hop substitutes is recommended, and the abolition of extraordinary tithes on hop land when turned to other uses.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

The medical inspection of school children in War- rington has not advanced very much. At the last meeting of the Medical Inspection of School Children Sub-committee of the Education Authority, it was decided that the Health Committee be asked state what officers they purpose providing, and what their ditties will be for carrying out the inspection, and what portion of the work they require to be carried out by the Education Committee. * * New Zealand can hardly be said to have covered itself with glory in the matter of a memorial to the most famous of its Prime Ministers, the late Mr. Seddon. The final meeting of the committee has just been held, and the sum total of the public subscrip- tions was reported to be £1,238, and £lOO of this sum came from the railwaymen, in whose ranks Ur. Seddon started his Colonial career. The Government is going to supplement the public subscription in order to provide a decent statue. One hundred thousand pounds and a grand technical college was the original idea. _ * * * The velocity of 1,410 yards per minute attained by the winning pigeon in the great Lancashire race from Nantes this week is a remarkable achievement, but it by no means constitutes a record in pigeon-flying. South America claims to hold the record with velo- cities of over 2,000 yards a minute —almost 1 1-7 miles a minute,or 68 miles an hour. English pigeon- flyers are inclined to discount these achievements, like some other American records. In pigeon-flying, however, a great deal depends on the weather and the condition of the atmosphere. Given clear air, a pigeon will do twice as well as he will in a slight mist. It is hard to get an English day absolutely free from mist. *

The Access to Mountains Bill has been withdrawn for the time being. The defenders of property have fought it tooth and nail, as if the object of the Bill were some horrible menace. The Lord Advocate had a word of warning that was very pertinent: He had the strongest opinion that if the landed interests of this country were to be found in conflict with those general rights of the public of access to the mountains, moors, and streams of our country—and the access also to its sea shores— theu,iudeed, the land rights themselves were standing in a position of serious peril. We hope that the Government may be able (next year, if possible) either to introduce or to help forward a Land Bill of this kind. Personally we shall continue to claim access to any mountains which may appeal to our fancy. * * * The great Wesleyan petition in favour of the Licensing Bill, which was more than a rival to the petition presented against it some• time ago, was brought into the House of Commons on Tuesday. It was borne up the floor of the House on a trolley with india-rubber tyres, and the ceremony of presenting it had been rehearsed before the House met, so that there might be no hitch. Ur. A. Henderson ,first wheeled the trolley half-way up the floor of the House amid loud cheers, and then from his place read the prayer of the petition. The Speaker invited the hon. member to bring as much of it to the table as was possible, and this having been done, the attendants wheeled the trolley out of the Chamber. The petition had been brought to the House from the office of the Temperance Legislation Society, and its progress through the streets attracted considerable attention. * * * Many of our readers will rejoice to hear that Mr. Louis F. Post, the editor o 1" The Public," Chicago, is shortly to visit this country. Mr. Post, who for many years was Henry George's right hand, has been delegated by the American Free Trade League to represent them at the International Free Trade Congress, to be held in London from the 4th to 7th of , August. Mr. Post will arrive in Liverpool lon July 25 or 26, and will proceed to London via Manchester, Birmingham, and Oxford. On his I return journey he purposes visiting York, Edinburgh, and Glasgow, whence be will embark for New York on August 15th by a steamer of the Anchor Line. Land Reformers will welcome the opportunity of making the personal acquaintance and paying their respects to one of the staunchest and most able men the movement has produced. * * Mr. Sydney Buxton, who visits Warrington next Thursday, to open the new Post Office, may be fairly ' styled the most progressive Postmaster-General that the G.P.O.has ever had. It would take up quite a lot of space to enumerate all the reforms and concessions for which lie has been responsible, while be has con- trived at the same time to secure in an exceptional degree the goodwill of the vast staff which he directs. Mr. Buxton bogan his public career at an early age, having been elected a member of the London School Board soon after.he had attained his majority, and he has many -interests to which he is devoted. Oa questions of finance, rating, and taxation he is specially strong, and he has been credited with a con- siderable share of responsibility for the death duties, for he assisted Sir William Harcourt in the production of the Budget which introduced this impost. In addition Mr. Buxton is a keen sportsman, who can shoot a driven partridge and throw a dry fly better than most of his contemporaries. * * The Parents' League—that mysterious organisation which has been heard of nearer home—held a meet- ing at Queen's Hall on Monday night, at. which Mr. Balfour was the principal speaker. Lord Salisbury, in the chair, struck what may be called the keynote of the meeting by declaring that " the principle of the League was the maintenance of the right of the parent to determine the religions education ot his children in elementary schools.' Could any language possibly be more inexact ? You cannot " maintain " some- thing which does not exist, and this " right " of the parent will have to be first of all secured before it can be maintained. It certainly does not exist at present. Ins Welsh village there ma/ be fifty Non-conformist children out of (say) 100 attending (and compelled to attend) a Church school, but the Nonconformist parents have not the smallest " right "to determine the religious teaching their children get. They are merely offered the choice of Church teaching or no religious teaching at all. * * The results of the recent preliminary examination for the certificate—or the King's Scholarship, as it used to be called—are very gratifying as far as Warrington is concerned. All the candidates pre- sented—St —passed. One gained distinction in five subjects, one in three subjects, two in two, and six id one. Twenty-two have been accepted for admission t) Training Colleges. This is the first time since the opening of the centre that the percentage of passes has reached 100: Last year it was 95 2. The follow- ing comparison is interesting :—Number of,Warring- ton students accepted for admission to Training Colleges, 18 out of 51 examined in 1904; 5 out of 23 examined in 1905 • 15 out of 23 examined in 1900; 16 out of 21 examined in 1907; 22 out of 34 examined in 1908. The School Management Committee has resolved that an expression of their satisfaction at the result of the examination be conveyed to the Head- master of the Secondary School and to the teachers concerned.

The Education Committee is taking steps to pat into operation the Provision of Meals Act 1900, A School Canteen Committee has beea.formed, and meals will be served to selected neCessitous children in the elementary schools. Parents will do well to study the conditions printed on page six. They are not obe relieved of parental responsibility. The scheme as outlined seems to be sensible and workmanlike. Public subscriptions are desired. The 'Pembroke election result will probably be mere gratifying to Liberals than Conservatives, though the latter claim to have reduced the majority by 1,000 votes. Mr. Roch M.P.'s majority is 2,174, against 3,280 in the 1905 Free Trade election. It is quite good enough as it stands, but to check any undue Tory elation, it is worth while pointing out that the Liberal poll is higher than it was in 1895, or 18A while the Conservative poll is lower. Tariff Reform has not made the slightest headway in SoutiOVales,even though" tin has gone," as Mr. Chamberlain once rashly asserted.

* * * In his review of the position of the Post Office Department in the House of Commons on Thursday the Postmaster General (Mr. Sydney Burton) regretted "from a postal point of view " that the limerick craze was disappearing. In the ordinary way the public would have bought during the last six months 700,000 or 800,000 sixpenny postal orders, but instead they had purchased no fewer than 11,400,000. Mr. Buxton caused much laughter by adding that he thought of offering a very substantial prize for some other public craze which would pass the scrutiny of the Anti-gambling League and the Manchester Watch Committee.

* * * From reports to band „it is evident (writes a "Manchester Guardian " correspondent) that, there is likely to be one of those rare invasions of our country this season by that native of Asia,Pallas's sandgrouse, for a number of these-beautiful birds have been seen in places as far apart as Norfolk, Essex, and Surrey. When last they came West in this way they were seen in many parts of Lancashire and,Cheshire. The bird is not unlike a golden plover in flight, but may easily be distinguished by its long tail and, if the observer is near enough, by the beauty of its markings. It will be well to keep a sharp look-out for them, as it may be years before a strange impulse brings these Eastern strangers to us again. * * * Our contemporary, the "Observer "—otherwise the Publican's Friend —said on Saturday that the "Examiner" had been "true to its traditions." This was not intended to be complimentary, but we feel flattered nevertheless. The "Observer " quarrels with us because of our statement that "drunken men are served with drink by the publicans every night that passes, or we should not see so much drunkenness in our streets." We are not surprised that the " Obseryer " should contend there is not the slightest foundation for such a serious charge against the publicans as a body." They also have to be true to their traditions, and tradition says that brewers' money and the " Observer " have long been well acquainted. . For ourselves, we remain unrepentant. What we have said we have said !

* * All this is very elementary, and we (says the Westminster Gazette") are almost ashamed to have to set it all out for the hundredth time; but we have no option when we see the " right of the parent " treated as something in existence, of which a wicked Radical and Nonconformist Government is trying to rob a parent if he happens to be a. Churchman. The truth is that the " right of the patent " is a " platformula." Ur. Balfour, referring to tests tr teachers, said : That was made, ram well aware, a shibboleth of the platform, but it is a shibboleth quite useless r except on the platform. ,It carries with it no clear or definite meaning to any thinking man, and its whole object and effect is to call clown cheers at the moment and possibly to obtain votes. This is really true of the shibboleth of the " right " of the parent. It was invented in order to justify the destruction of the Education Bill of 1900 by Mr. Balfour and the House a Lords. To prevent miscon- ception, we do not say that the wishes of the parents should not be respected as far as possible. But that is a wholly different thing from saying that the parent has at present a "right" to denominational teaching, which the Church is trying to " maintain " and the Liberal party to get rid of.

About 150 left I the Central Station at eight o'clock and lunch was ' served en route. When Stratford-on-Avon was reached 1 at one o'clock rain was falling heavily and continued 1 for the remainder of the day, considerably marring the success of the outing. The various places of interest were viewed including Shottery, Ann i Hathaway's Cottage, Shakespeare's birth place, the memorial theatre, Shakespeare's grave in Stratford Church, the fine American memorial to the great poet, and Miss Marie Corelli's residence. The return journey was commenced at 6.15 and dinher was pro- vided en route. Warrington was reached about 11 I o'clock.

div.head: CROSFIELD'S BAND AT BELLE VUE.
div.p: CROSFIELD'S BAND AT BELLE VUE.

In the twenty-third annual July brass band festival, held at the Belle Vue Gardens, Manchester, on Saturday, twenty bands took part. The competitors were drawn largely from the mining and industrial I districts of Lancashire and Yorkshire. Although the weather in the afternoon was bad there was a big I attendance. The earnest interest of the large crowd in the fortunes of the respective bands was shown by the thousands who filled the large hall where tho Icompetition took place. The contest was con- fined to amateur bands which had not won a prize during the past two years in the Belle Vue September contests, and on this oePasion the test piece was again an arrangement by Lieutenant Charles Godfrey of a selection from Hermann Goetz's comic lopera a The Taming of the Shrew." Messrs. W. IShort (bandmaster to the London County Council), and J. W. Beswick of Manchester), were the adjudi- cators. —The awards were as follows :—First prize, £2O, Crosfield's Soap Works, Warrington, conductor W. Halliwell ; second, .£l2 Stalybridge Borough, Alex. Owen ; third, XS, Le; Mills (Matlock Bath), Alex. Owen ; fourth, £l, Nelson Old, W. Halliivell; fifth, Dennemora Steel Works, Sheffield, E. Richford. It was announced that Monday, September 7, had been fired for the annual championship contest at Belle Vue.

The season's suocasses up-to-date are as follows : Four Ist prizes, three 2ad prizes, two 3rd prizes, out of nine contests attended. Comparison with the best contesting bands show very favourable results, and marks strongly the advancement which the Band is making:46— .

div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
A COLLIER'S CHILD NEGLECE

I Harry Hart, a collier, of Golborne, was sent to gaol at the Warrington Petty Sessions on Wednesday for three months on a charge of neglecting to maintain his daughter, whereby she became cnargeable to the funds of the Leigh Union. It was stated that. the child had been twice admitted into the Leigh Workhouse. The prisoner had made no effort to support the child, whose maintenance in the Union had coat the ratepayers some- thing like £5O.

div.head: ASSAULTING A LANDLORD.
div.p: ASSAULTING A LANDLORD.

James Daffy, pit contractor of Station-road,Haydack, was summoned at Newton Sessions last Thursday for refusing to quit the Ram's Head, Haydock, and also for assaulting Thomas Thomley, the landlord. Mr. Knowles for the prosecution, said Mr. Thomley was very strict in the management of his house, and forbade any woman with a child in arms being served with more than one drink. In accordance with that rule Daffy's wife was refused a second drink, and Daffy thereupon abused Mr. Thomley, refused to leave, and finally assaulted him. Mr. Thomley deposed that a report was made to him by Miss Scott, his barmaid, and he told Daffy andhis wife they could not have any more drink. Duffy used a nasty expression and took up a threatening attitude. Witness pushed him out but he returned, seized him by the collar, pulled him off the doorstep, and then got hold of his leg and threw him down. Witness held him off as well as he could without striking him, and was kicked by somebody while struggling.—Walter Boatty, clerk in Messrs. Richard Evans and Ca's office, P.C. Turner, and Miss Scott, the barmaid, corroborated and the defendant, who did not appear, was fined Os. and costs. ROBBING THE HEN-ROOST.

At Newton Petty Sessions last Thursday, Michael Mitchell and William Broxen pleaded guilty to a charge of stealing five fowls worth 143., the property of Harvey Burman, farmer, Newton Common.—Plaintill's son identified some feathers as resembling those of some missing fowls.—Police-Sergeant B wow said he heard of the fowls being taken from Mr. 13urrarna's, and found that the fowl house doors had been forced open. He traced blood and feathers towards Cherry-street, where Mitchell's mother lives. He asked Mrs. Mitchell what was in a pan on the flre,and she said nothing but hot ' water; but there were portions of fowl in it,and he found other parts, and some feathers, partly burnt. There was blood on the prisoner's clothes,as wallas feathers.— Inspector Innes said these were idlo mea—pests to the neighbourhood.—Both men objected to the Inspector's description of them, and Mitchell said he worked when he was out of gaol.—The Chairman said Broxen had been before the Bench 15 times and Mitchell four times. The Bench fined them 20s. and cats each, or a month, and greatly appreciated Sergt. Barrow's services in tracing them.

FLAT CAP CAIN DROWNED.

iMr. S. Brighouse held an inquest at Widnes on ; Monday on Charles Mellor, 47, a river fiat captain, who was thrown overboard as the result of a collison I between two flats. A rope was thrown to him, but he failed to grasp it and went down. The jury returned a ; verdict of " Accidental death."—Mr. Byfield, of the Grappling Corps, in reply to the Coroner, said that during the six years' existence of the corps, they have I-recovered 36 bodies ; 13 this year. Their services were , requisitioned all over the country. They had not got ! very liberal financial support, and their funds were in a low state.—The Coroner said it was a Christian work ' and one which ought to commend itself to the people. It was a great solace to relatives when bodies were recovered so that they could have Christian burial. THRASHED CONTINUALLY. RUNCORN WIFE'S BITTER COMPLAINT.

At Runcorn, on Monday, Albert Lloyd,of Bold-street, was summoned by his wife, Mary E. Lloyd, of Green- way-road, for desertion. On the appliztion of Mr. Burton, the case was adjourned for a =VI; remarking that he anticipated a settlement. John Welsh, a young man of Surrey-street, was sum- moned for persistent cruelty to his wife, Edith. Mrs. Welsh said she had been married nineteen months, and there was no family. Ever since she had been married, she had carried more black flesh than white. He had thrashed her continually. He did not get up until ten or eleven o'clock and would not work. Martha Butter, the mother of the complainant, described the scandalous condition of her daughter through the ill-treatment of the defendant. She had had to help to keep the defendant and his wife since they had been married. The bench granted a separation order, with Gs. a week alimony. WIDNES-LIBERAL CLUB. OBJECTED TO HEft SON'S COURTSHIP. Bridget Feeney, a middle-aged woman, of 13, Heath- street, 'Matto Heath, was ciaarged at St. Helens, on Saturday, with attemptinz to commit suicide by throw- ing herself through i. window.—The evidence was that the woman had been annoyed by one of her sons courting a girl of whom sae did not approve. His mother had made several scenes in the house, and had been taking a good deal of drink. On Friday the young man said as would leave the house. He went upstairs and packed his clothes. His mother followed, and had to be restrained or she would have jumped our, of the window. In coose4oence of her excited con- dition she was locked up.—Mrs. Feeney now said that she did not intend to do anything rash. She only wanted her son to stay at horue.—The woman's married daughter came forward, and said that her brother had given up the girl that his mother objected to, and that she would look after her mother.--The defendant was handed over to the care of Miss Scott, the lady

-BATCH OF MOTORISTS FINED. James Williams, chauffeur to Dr. Jackson, was sum- moned at St. Helens on Monday for driving a motor car at a dangerous speed in Prescot-road on Tuesday afternoon, the 7th inst. The police said he was going at least twenty miles an Lour. Chief Constable Elleringtoa said he saw the motor, and its speed was highly dangerous. Albert Broughton, who was driving a motor car on the same road, and Thomas Middle- hurst, who was riding Ns. ith him, said the car was not going more thin sixteen or eighteen miles au hour. Dr. Jackson said the defendant was a most careful and skilful driver. —Williams admitted that he would probably be going at eighteen miles an hour.—The Cnairman said that. would be a dangerous speed for the place, and the driver would to fined .C 1 and 10a. 6d. costs.—Antoiue Valen- ciennes, a Swiss engineer, and manager of the Motor Block Manufacturing Company, at Sutton Oak, was charged with driving at dangerous speed in Sutton- road. A policeman said the speed was thirty miles an hour. Defendant was the motor expert at these works, and tried the cars at terrific speeds on the roads in this neighbourhood.—Mr. A. E. Tickle, for the defence, said defendant had for six years driven in Italy, Germany, France, and Switzerland without the slightest complaint or accident.—Fined 203. and costs.—Charles John Edward^. Deansgate, Manchester, who said he was taking a car to the Motor Block Works, was charged with driving at a dangerous speed up Peasley Cross- lane.—Fined £5 and la 3s. 6d. costs. sr. HELENS MINERS' DISPUTE. 1,100 MEN ON STRIKE. A serious state of affairs now exists in connection with the Ashton's Green Collieries, St. Helens, belong- ing to Messrs. 13ronailow, Forster, and Co., where eleven hundred men came out on strike on Tuesday. The trouble is solely confined to a dispute between the men oiemselves. Close on eleven hundred of the awn are members of the Miners Federation ; but for some time a few of the employees have resisted all the efforts of their fellows to induce them to join the union, and as the majority refuse to work at a pit where non-union mea are employed the strike has taken. place, although notices had beau served three weeks ago On Tuesday the men brought out their tools, and the position is di the raost serious description. An oiacial of the lirm stated that the firm have so far not been considered in the matter. They have no dispute and no grievance with the men and they desire that their collieries shall go on working in the usual way. They consider it somewhat hard on their firm that the pits !should be stopped through no fault of their own. A St. Helens correspondent says :—ln addition to the strike of colliers at St. Helens, the whole of the ironmoulders in the district ceased work on Tuesday night, the strike being against the proposed reduction by the masters of 3s. per week. The 3s. advance was given some time ago, and the masters now seek to with- draw it. The men's notices expired on Tuesday night, but negotiations are in progress with a view to settling , the matter.

At the Ravenshead Plate Glass Works between fifty and sixty of the employees are reported to have got notice to cease work, and it is feared that the whole of the works will in a short time be at a standstill. Sr. HELENS CORPORATION AND TRADES UNIONS. • • •

At the meeting of the',lS-C.-iieTens Parks Committee on Wednesday, Mr. H. H. Peet presiding, the Deputy Town-clerk reported that two letters had been received from thedocat branch of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants. In the first letter the secretary said :—" I desire to point out to you that, with regard to the question raised by Mr. \Vardle in the House of Commons re meetings, neither myself nor any of our members have any connection with this." The second letter stated :—" Your reply to my application for Val use of the Town Hall was placed before my Enembers,and I was instructed to ask your Council to again consider te charge you propose to make, which I may say I more than we can pay. We have eighteen meetings per year, and the police court room or a room not carpeted would meet our requirements. In our opinion this would not entail any extra Senday duty,as the constable on duty could unlock the room, and we would be responsible for any damage." The letter went on to state that the society was called upon to support orphr-is, &c., and that during the last fifteen years over £6OO had been paid for orphans in St. Helens alone, ' and they offered 2s. per week for a room.—After discus- sion it was decided to send the matter forward to the Watch Committee with a view to allowing the society the use of a room in connection stith the police depart- ment.

div.head: FEEDING OF SCHOOL CHILDREN. -- Scheme for Working tha Act in Warrington.
div.p: FEEDING OF SCHOOL CHILDREN. -- Scheme for Working tha Act in Warrington.

1 The Warrington Education Committee will at its [monthly meeting on Monday evening be asked to approve the following scheme submitted by the School Attend- ance Committee for putting the Education (Provision' of Meals) Act, 1900, into operation in this Borough viz :

(1) That a School Canteen Committoe be established to administer the Act ' • and that the School Attendance Committee be constituted as that Committee,. with power to co-opt additional members to be approved by the Education Com- mittee ; (2) that breakfast or dinner or both meals be pro- vided as each case may necessitate ; (3) that the meals be prepared at a centre, and that it be recommended that Garven Cottage will ba suitable for such centre ; • (4) that the meals be served in the public elementary schools; and that the Committee provide utensils; (5) that the school keepers be made responsible for the supervision of the children during meal Om( - • (l) that the pros ision of mealdbe confined to school days ; (7) that, with a view to discovering the most salt- able cases, the following mode of procedure be adopted, viz : (a) that head teachers be asked to furnish lists of the children who, in their opinion, need feeding ; () these cases to be investigated by the school attendance inspectors ; (c) the director and a member of the School Canteen Committee to be empowered, after consultation with the school medical (Wien' II hen necessary, to finally determine the cases ; and .. (a) the parents to be noti3ed beforehand of the Committee's Intention to feed their children. (S) that alt cases be reported to the weekly rota Committee for their consideration : (9) that meals be supplied to necessitous and neglected children only; and that the cases be clossitled as follows, viz. : (i) the children of parents who are in receipt of Poor Law relief ; (ii) the children of satisfactory parents who cannot feed their children owing to tempo- rary distress ; (iii) the children of unsatisfactory parents who cannot feed their children ; (iv) the children of unsatisfactory parents who can feed their children but negle:t to do so; that for the present, children in class (i) be not fed, but that any case of underfeeding be reported to the Guardians ; that children in class (iii) be fed, but that steps be at once tlken to make the parents feed them; that children in class (ir) be fed, but that the parents be proceeded against under the Preven- tion of Cruelty to Children Act ; (10) that, for the purpose of determining upon the necessitous cases, the following scale be follower?, the amount being calculated upon the gross income of the family after deducting the rent, viz. : (a) where there are one or two children, the income to be not more than 3s. per head of the children only; (b) where there are three or four children, the income to be not more than 2s. 9d. per head of the children only; (c) where there are five or more children, the income to be not more than 2s. 6d. per head of the children only; No child shall he fed free if the parent is in full employment and receiving the recognized local rate of pay for his class of work. (11) that, with a view; to obtaining money for the pro,- vii4ion of food, a public appeal be made.

div.p: WILMINGTON B3Y'S ADVENTURES. Result of Reading " Penny Dreadfuls."

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday, John William Jeffries (161, We'field-street. was charged with stealing from the (lwelling-hrmse, 41, Price-street, a number of books and a quantity of food. A fortnight nrgo the h.)y was found, protrently destitute, in a field by n Mrs. 'Ntarehment, IL Price-street. She took him home. fed hire, clothed him, and gave him lodgings. lie stated he had work to go to, but would not get paid until July 11th. On Saturday Mrs. March ment went to the seaside for the day, and while she was away Jeffries broke into the house and stole three reading books, a boy's jacket, butter, cheese, and eight P2C9. lie was found cooking the eggs by a relative of Mr+. Marchment, who went in. Before leaving Jeffries left the following note on the table : " I have not been working this fo-tnight. I WAS offered a job, brit could not get it. I hope you will forgive me. Very sorry. I have enjoyed myself more at your house than ever I have eneware in my live. lam going on the road to Manchester to find work, and when I get it will repay Yon for all yon have dove for me. I have toke some bread and butter." Jeffries told the magistrates that he aid not take all the things mentioned in the charge. Ile bad left four eggs for the lodger. Pristmer's father slid he apprenticed his son at Dallarn Forge, hut three weeks ago he was instantly dismissed, as be had neglected his employment. On Walking Day wiPness WV him having his tea with the Salvation Army in the Park, but he made off and ant- raced witness. He btd been informed by his son's former employer that prisoner was eontinnnllv reading "penny horribles" instead of working, and witness had found a harrowful of them at home. On prisoner promising to give no rending trash litera- ture, and to reform, the Bench allowed him to go home under the care of his father.

CHURCH SCZCD.VY SCHOOL TEACHERS' A S-10CTITIONT. —The nnnnal garden party in connection with the Warrington Branch of this association, which is always held at Padgate in July, took place on Saturday last, hut was sadly marred hy rain. The Vicarage grounds were looking their hest and many mimes had been Pre- pared for the visitors inclnding a " nutting course " for golf,but, with the excent ion of a few rounds of the latter. all were a`andoned. An excellent tea was served in the school, and at 7 p.m., a short service was held in Christ Church when an address was given by the Rev. A. F. White. of Hollinfare. TITE IVEST.EY Gc rt.P.—On Monday evening a meeting of this guild was held on Dr. Tiennet'slawn. Additional interest was evinced in the gathering owing to the fact that this wrs the last occasion on which the present president (the Rev. William Mellor`, who will shortly conclude his ministry in the Warrington Circuit, would occupy the chair. Alderman Bennett gave an address on "Some reminiscences of the old Padzate Wesleyan Chapel." He gave an interesting account of the old chapel and recilled many incidents which took place within its walls, reminding his bearers of many persons —both worshippers and ministers—who once resorted there, hot who had since passed away. The Rev. George H. Riggall. of Birmingham. spoke of "Mission work in the slnms." The Rev. %V. Mellor spoke of the pleasure be had derived from the Guild meetings during the past ' three years. lie trusted that God would bless them, and that they would go on with increasing success.

Thomas Snelson, a NViredrawer. of Warrington, and .Tames Lomas, described as a stoker, of ManeLeiter. who were remanded for inquiries at Northwich a week ago on a charge of stealing a pair of men's boots, value 3s. 11d., the property of the Cash Boot Com- pany, lwanse of Lomas's refusal to give any aeconnt of himself, :wain appeared before Messrs. J. W. Deakin (chairman) and T. B. Aforetoa on Monday.— The magistrates were of opinion that Snelson Lad been led into trouble by Lomas. Lomas would there- fore have to go to gaol for two months' bard labour and Snelscn for one m.,nth Nv ith hard labour.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council .was held at thl Independent Llbour Party room, Friars' Green, on Tuesday evening. Mr. W. If. Richardson presiding over a fair attendance which included the Secretary (Mr. E. Plinston).

div.head: COUNCILLOR STOTT 00iND TO NEW ZEALAND.
div.p: COUNCILLOR STOTT 00iND TO NEW ZEALAND.

The SECRETARY read a letter from Councillor Fred Stott stating that Mrs. Stott and himself had decided to emigrate to New Zealand. He asked for a letter signed by the ofUcials and executive of the Trades Council giving a brief record of his connection with and work on behalf of the Council during big ten years as a delegate thereto. It might help him to secure friends in what would he to him a strange country. He hoped to be present at the August meeting to bid all old collennes " good-bye." , The Council readily acceded to Councillor Stott's request.
VOTES FOR 'WOMEN. !MOULD VIE A.GITATORS BE TREATED AS POLITICAL OFFENDERS? .

The Woolwich Trieles—nici-I:Abonr Council wrote asking the Council to endorse the following resolution: --" That the Woolwich District Trades and Labour Council enters a strong protest against the treatment of the women who were imprisoned for acts committed during their political struggle for the enfranchisement of women and calls on his Majesty's Government to bring the women 83 imprisoned under the category of political prisoners." In an accompanying letter the Secretary of the Council stated: That they should be treated as common criminals and not as political offenders is to my Council an indication of the means that would be adopted by the present or any other capitalistic Government to crush any movement of the workers with which they did not agree." Mr. Ptumrs moved that the Council endorse the 1 resolution, lie believed the women were making a strenuous light for a principle that was right. Our forefathers bad to fight very hard to gain the vote for men, and he failed to sea why women shoald not have the same privileges that the men possessed. Mr. Maven seconded.

Mr. THORNLEY moved thst the letter lie on the table. He thought the conduct of some of these women was disgrace to their sex. Before the Council battled for women's votes they should go in for adult suffrage. Mr. T. Sm grit was of the same opinion. livery man when he attained his majority should be entitled to a vote, and when that pint was gained it would be time to see about votes for women.

Mr. ALONE pointed out that the resolution had nothing to do with the principle of votes for women but simply protested against the agitators being treated as common criminals. Mr. Sesta maintained that the women were not sent to prison as politicl offenders. They bad broken the civil law and he did not think they were getting one bait their due. He was sorry the old-fashioned "ducking stool" had been done away with. He did not insinuate that woman was on a lower level than man but they ought to gain adult suffrage first and then votes for women if they liked. He, however, strongly opposed the agitators in question being treated other- wise than as common prisoners. If a poor woman stole to satisfy the hunger of herself and family, she would be sent to prison and she had more right to do that than these women had to smash the Prime Minister's windows. _

Mr. PLUMB thought the women ought to be allowed to use their own discretion to some extent as to which were the best methods. If they thought they could advance the cause by breaking the Prime Minister's windows, he did not think the Council need trouble much about that.

Mr. BULLOCK said he did not wish to say anything detrimental to the movement but he considered the methods of the agitators were ridiculous. On a vote being taken the amendment that the letter lie on the table was carried by 8 votes to 6. L kNCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE FEDERATION. _

The Sserteirertleas the representative of the Council on the Education Committee, presented his annual report oa the work of the authority. He said there had been much criticism respecting the authority and its I work, strong condemnation AS to the cost of administra- tion, without proper and full acknowledgment of the results accomplished. When they remembered that prior to the present Act becoming operative, there was I not only hick of school accommodation hut a corres- ponding shortage in the staffing of the schools that did exist. and monetary burdens which in some cases were far beyond the p 'wets of the managers to cope with, low salaries to te where which oft times meant inefficiency, there was every cause for satisfaction that so many of those difficulties hal been overcome at a cost comparatively light as compared with other towns. Warrington stood amongst the lowest as to cost of ftdministration,and in the list of highest for educational results. Although rapid strides had been made, much work remained to be done, and that of a meat important nature. Farther school accommoda- tion must be provided • many schools were much overcrowded and adversely reported npon by the Government inspectors on that account. Steps were being taken, w:rich he trusted would not be unduly delayed, for the erection of additional bnildines, and they had reason to be proud of the Beamont and Bolton Schools. Mr. Plinston then referred to the Feeding of School Children Act, and said that in its administration they would have to differentiate between the parents who could not, owing to the temporary stoppage of work or slackness in trade, provide food for their children, and those who apparently cared little whether they worked or not. fa both cases the children most be fed, but in the Letter case steps would have to be taken to compel the parents to provide the necessary cost. The great weakness in the Act was that authori- ties were compelled fist to endeavour to obtain the necessary funds by voluntary off n.t. and failing this, then, through the Board of Elucation, Town Councils would have the power to levy a rate of not more than one helfpeany in the £ for the carrying out of the work., Surely this should be the duty of the State, seeing that the Siete compelled the attendance of children at school.
