ILDREII,

I have much pleasure in forwarding the prizes for the best conundrums to M. Faulk- ner, Gerald Appleby, Maud Mobley, and Amelia Erisley. I have been very pleased, indeed, with the number of replies I received in this compe- tition.

Isn't it curious that cut of all the picture poatcarda received only four, up to the present, have given the date of my birthday? I must thank my members for the many kind messages received. If I do not receive another correct one during the week, I shall give the P.O.'s for E.s. to the fonr correct ones.

Don't forget the announcement of the "Holi- day Competition." Durity, July, I want you to send me your idea of an ideal holiday. To the sender of the best I shall give a P.O. for 55., and tO the second best 2s. 6d.

Think what you would like best to do for a menth during the summer with plenty of money. This should not be very difficult. If I had the time and money, I think I would wan- der through the country parts of France, Bel- gium, and Italy. What would you do? I hope to bave a large number of replies during July. Good bye for another week. With love, UNCLE NED.

Welcome to Amy Pickering, Agnes Giddy, Annie Giddy, Nellie Giddy, Olive Giddy, Lilian Dark, Bertie Finale Elsie White, Nellie Walsh, Rose Franklin, Hilda Ives,. Caroline Cheehire, Gladys Glibery, Daisy Swain, Doris Eayrs.
VICTORIA CROSS.

Having often been asked this question, and as I believe the circumstances are peculiar and unique, the following account of the matter is herewith truthfully recorded. It was at Lucknow, during the terrible sum- mer of 1859, when our poor soldiers, who had just captured that city, were dying like flies of heat-apoplexy, and the Great Comet was blazing in the sky. On one day the 38th Regiment, which was encamped near the town, lost nine- teen men from that scourge alone. A famous General, whose name could never be mentioned by a native without a giggle, was commanding the station and cantonment at that time; a genial, excellent officer, with perhaps the strongest Milesian accent ever heard out of Tipperary. The story used to run that a wag- gish subaltern inquired innocently, one day from the Chief, "if he had ever been in Ire- land?" "Oi was there warnce I" rolled out of the ready roguish lips. He sent for me in a great hurry one morning,, and I found him in his orderly-room, bathed in perspiration, with his swora girt around him, but otherwise attired in the lightest and most casual official costume permissible to one of such exalted rank. By his request, I seated myself opposite to him, at a little table covered with documents and despatches. "Sure, it's awful hot weather," said the General, mopping his forehead. To which I re- spectfully assented, wondering what desperate deed might be required of me. "Sure, they've sent this out from England for me to give ye," laying his hand on a little cardboard box. I bowed, still wondering.

"I'm told to parade all the troops in garri4 son (some 2,000 men) for that purpose. But, sure, the weather's awful hot. Would ye be so kind as to forego the parade?" By this time a dawning of his meaning had flashed upon me, and I heartily replied, "Most certainly, sir!" "Sure, it's very good of ye." Then, after an embarrassed pause, "Will you take it from me here?"

"If you please, sir." "And, sure, there it is," said the Chief, evi- dently much relieved, as he handed the little box to me across the table. I pocketed it, shook hands with him, and came away, the for- tunate possessor of a much-prized Victoria, Cross.

When he was seen by none, And chased and killed his duckling—
Just for fun. When master found what mischief
That naughty dog had done, He said that he must beat him— Just for fun. __

TOO MUCH FOR THEM. Some years ago, while visiting the Spokanes, General Philip Sheridan related to the Indians, through an interpreter, the wonders of the rail- way, and then waited to see what effect the re- velation would have upon them. "What do they say?" he asked the inter- preter. "They say they don't believe it," was the answer. Sheridan then described the steam-boat, and the. interpreter repeated this. "What do they say to that?" the General asked again, seeing the Indian faces all im- passive. "They say they don't believ3 that either." Then the General gave an account of the tele- phone and told how a man at the end of a long wire had talked to a. man at the other end of it. The interpreter remained silent. "Well," said the General, "why don.'t you interpret that to them?" "Because " answered the conscn,ntious man.
"Because I don't believe that story myself,"
GOOD NIGHT. Good night, good night, the day is slowly dying. Home flits the swallow to the cottage eaves; . . .

A little wind creeps through the -woodland, sighing, And dies among the leaves. The red deer seeks the bracken in the dingle, The flocks are couching on their beds of thyme; Far off, a long wave rolls upon the shingle, And sings its sleepy rhyme. Oh, rest in peace! our angel guards, unsleeping, Watch o'er the homes where languid sorrow lies; After the darkness of a night of weeping, The morn of joy shall rise! Good night, good night; in quiet chambers kneeling, We pray for our beloved ones out of sight; There comes an answer througlx_ the cool air stealing, "God bless you, love, good night l" When are your teeth like your tongue ? QUESTIONED IN FOUR LANGUAGES.

A story is told of a country coroner who was called upon to hold an inquest over the body of an Italian. The only witness was a small boy of the same nationality, who spoke no English. The examination proceeded thus:— "Where do you live, my boy?" The by shook his head. "Do you speak English!" Another shake of the head. 'Do you speak French?" Another shake. "Do you speak German?" Still no answer. "How old are you!" No reply. "Do you speak Italian!"

The lioy give no sign. "Well," said the coroner, "I have questioned the witness in four languages, and can get no answer. It is useless to proceed. The Court is adjourned until further evidence can be ob- tained."

The clickity, clackity, meddlesome clock Looked at the fairy, saying "Tick, tock." "Why," said the fairy, "don't you know? I've come to mend the hole in the toe." The fairy soon mended the little boy's sock: "That's very well done," said the meddlesome

clock. Away flew the fairy, full of great joy, Out of the window, after kissing the boy. Hurrah!" said the cliekity, clackity clock. "The oranges, figs, and peppermint rock Cannot possibly tumble out of the toe; The fairy has mended the sock, you know" " Well, I declare!" said the meddlesome clock, " The fairy has widened the little boy's sock. How kind of. the fairy, when mending the-toe, To widen the gocß, when hurrying so!" When Santa Clims came, this meddlesome clock Pointed its hand straight at the sock. The old man saw what the fairy had done; He filled it with gifts, enjoying the fun! "Tick, tock," said again the meddlesome clock. The term " Inland Correspandenco " means cor- respondence posted within the United Kingdom, iwiluding the Isle of Man and the Co time! Islands. "Inland Correspondence" is divided into the following classes : (a) Letters (d) Newspapers (b) Postcards (e) Parcels (c) Halfpenny packets Not only letters, bat any document or article (with a few trifling exceptions) which can be trans- mitted by post at all, may be sent by letter post, the only limitation being that of size. For every additional 2 0z5.... id. • A letter posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with double postage; a letter insulliciently paid, with double the deficiency. No letter may exceed two feet in length, one foot in width, or one foot in depth. POST-CARDS. The prepaid rate of postage on every post-card is one half-penny, and on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card posted unpaid is chargeable oz delivery with one penny. Cards used as post-cards must be made of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for the thickest official post-card. They may not exceed 5) inches in length by 3} inckes In width, or be loss than 31 inches in length by 21 inches in width. A gummed label (not to exceed 2 inches long and finch wide) bearing the address may now be itlxed to the address side of card. If any of the rides relating to a post-card be infringed, the card will be treated as a letter. _

The postage on a parcel must be prepaid. Mark each parcel Parcel Post." A parcel must not be posted in a letter box, but presented at the counter Of a post office, and the sender should see that the weight, size and postage are inorder before leaving. PARCELS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL). Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the Inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents must be declared. The custocas charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. The postage varies, to different countries and must be prepaid. MONEY ORDERS (INLAND.) The postal authorities cannot issue a:single money order for more than £4O, and will only cash them at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional part of a, id. can be contnined in a money order. The rates of poundage are :—Not exceeding £l, 23. ; £3, 3d.; £lO, 4d.; £2O, 6d.; £3O, Bd. ; £4O, 10d. By paying an additional 23. aud cost of the telegram of advice, a money order can be telegraphed under certain restrictions. MONEY ORDERS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.) The maximum amount for which a money order may be issued for places abroad varies in each particular place. The poundage rates are :—Not exceeding £1,33. ; £2, Gd. • and above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of GI. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to be telegraphed to certain places abroad. POSTAL ORDERS. • These are obtainable at any money order office in the United Kingdom, and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, rising by 6d., from 6d. to £1 Is. The poundage fees are :-13. up to 2s. ad.; Id. up to 155.; lid. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee filled in. The Post- master-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd. can be affixed to make up odd SUMS. TELEGRAMS (INLAND). The Postmaster-General possesses,almost entirely, the privilege of transmitting,colleoting and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. The charge for a telegram is a minimum amount of Gd. which covers 12 words, and an additional id. ior each extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if soot out for delivery from a head telegraph office, but if from a sub-office then within three miles only, beyond which a charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form. Address of person receiv- iog a telegram has to be paid for, but sender's name if written on back of form need not be. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply may be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in wall or pillar boxes, or handesi to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The cost of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must cousist of two words, is £1 Is. TELEGRAMS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL) Must be written on special forms and are accepted lii the language of any of the principal European countries. The rates vary, and are too numerous ' to detail here. P0:..,T OFFICE SAVINGS BANK. These are established at all money order offices. In ordinary cases the annual deposit must not exceed £5O, ani the total amount £.lOO. No person can have more than one account. Amounts placed in the bank on behalf of children under seven years of age cannot be withdrawn until the child reaches that ago, and then only under his or her own signa- ture. The smallest amount received at a time is Is., and this may take the form of 12 penny stamps affixed to a special form. Each depositor receives a bank book in which the cmonnt of each deposit should be entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is C 1 or over, a special acknowledgfient is sent from the head London office. Interest is allowed at the rate of 21 per cent. Any amount up to and including £t may be withdrawn without previous notice, on presenting a bank book. The bank book should be sent each year, postage free, on the anniversary of the date when the account was opened, to the Controller of the Savings Bank Department for purposes of checking and adding interest. The withdrawal of money can be expedited by telegraphing, the depositor paying cost of telegrams. P.O. TELEPHONE AND TRUNK LINE CHARGES. Erich driver must possess a license, costing 55., to be renewed every 12 months, and obtainable from the county authorities, which may he endorsed or suspended for reckless driving or certain other Offences. The highest speed at which a car may be driven on the public highways is 20 miles en hour, which is redaced to 10 miles under special local regula- tions. It is an offence nnder tho Motor Car Act (1003), to drive a car in such a way on n public highway as to be dargerous to the public, having regard to the circumstances of the ease. In the event of an accident to any person due to tho presence of the motor car on the road, the driver must supply his name and address, and the owner and number of the car, under heavy penal- ties. The driver must produce his licence at the request of a police constable.

div.head: EXCITING CHASE AFTER GAME TRESPASSERS.
div.p: EXCITING CHASE AFTER GAME TRESPASSERS.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before , Mr. William Long .(in the chair), and other magistrates, Isaac Smith, Manley-street, George Ogden, Dolman's- ', lane, and Peter, Itowson, Bowes-street, all of Warrin g- ton, were summoned for entering land in the daytime ' in the possession and occupation of Thomas Percival, at Moore, in search of game, without the consent of the owner. The defendants pleaded not k ttilty.—Mr. Browne prosecuted on behalf of Sir Richard Brooke,and said the °Renee was committed at Moss Side, Moore,at 3.30 on the morning of the 24th June. This was one of those cases in which the defendants crossed from Bank Quay, Warrington, in a boat to the land, : and it WAS very dillicult to catch them. Mr. Ernest Harold Lon, one of the keepers, was on land in the occupaticn of Mr. Bradbury when he saw three men about 150 yards away on land in the occupation of , Mr. Thomas Percival. He concealed himself in a hedge, and when the men got up to him he stopped them and said" I shall charge you with being on land in pursuit of game." They refused to allow him to searoh them. He attempted to get hold of Smith's bag, , when Ogden began to use a stick in a threatening ; manner. being one course it bein one man against three he had to let them go,and they got into a boat and rowed off,but , be wont to Warrington as quickly as possible and at tho I Police Station obtained the services of an officer, who I went with him to Quay Fold, I%here they saw the , boat containing three men. The police constable I shouted to Smith, "Oh ! Ike know you." j The men dodged about in the river and ultimately I succeeded in getting away from the keeper and the ! police officer. However Long was prepared to swear that the defendants were the three men he saw on the I land on the morning in questior. Ile (Mr. Browne) had been instructed to press the case as the conduct of the defendants and other Man wts a perfect nuisance to the 1 keepers, who had to be up night cud day to watch them coming from Bank Quay. I Evidence in support of the statement was given. I Alfred France said he was on the land on the morning in question and not Smith. There were two men with him. The magistrates retired foal the Court to con- sider their decision. On their return the chairman said , I the magistrates were unanimously of cpinion that the case was proved Defendants had a very i,lrch record,and , would each be fin A 20d. aid B own° api red ' for the advocate's fee, which was allowed.

div.head: PETER WALKER AND SONS LTD.
div.p: PETER WALKER AND SONS LTD.
Annual Excursion.

Hai the weather been rather more indulgent on Saturday last, the excursion to Morecambe of the e nployees and friends of the above firm, would have been all that could have been desired. About 1,590 persons left Warringt soon after 6.0 a.m., and the jubilant holiday makers reached their destination about 8 o'clock. Arrived at More- cambe each departed to his or her special attraction— the boats; the switchback; the flying machine, &e. Lancaster drew a good many of the visitors, who were very well satisfied with the various items of interest to be seen there. At 11 o'clock a good many found it convenient to go for a sail on either the Britannia or the Sunbeam, which were specially hired for the 'excursionists. Whilst out in the bay, it commenced to rain, and the saloons being full, a good many had to expexience that very undesirable feature of nature —a drenching. Three young men in desperation took refuge under the " look-out " and thus saved them- selves the trouble of having to get their clothes dried, when they got ashore, or go about feeling as if they had been bathing with their clothes , on. In the afternoon the Winter Gardens were the rendezvous of nearly all the trippers, and judging from their, faceq the admirable programme readered was mud; enjoyed. I In the evening, dinner was served to about fifty of the employees and friends, at the Girrad Hotel. After 1 it was over, toasts were given. Councillor Furiron-Siatrir in proposing the health of the King said that they looked to his Majesty with that partriotism and devotion becoming a Loyal people. They saw day by Oly the manifold blessings which pervaded the national life of the country. Mr. Smith then read a telegram from Mr. Monro, which expressed the hope that they would have an enjoyable outing. They fully appreciated Mr. Monro's senti- ment. They had found him a genial, good man, and it was with regret that they heard he had to retire on account of his health giving way. He (Mr. Smith) was ' sure that he was echoing the sentiments of all present when be said that they all wished him a speedy return to health.

The next toast was " The Queen and the Royal Family " which was honoured very heartily. Mr. W. H. J. JENKINS then proposed a toast to P. Walker and Sons, Limited. He said that he might vouch from his personal knowledge, that the men had Always been treated with proper consideration. He had also seen illustrations of the firm's kindness to the employees who needed help. He had ample proof of the same kindness extended by them to those who otherwise would not possibly have had a claim. He had approached them to extend charitable consideration to the little ones. He bad taken an Dative interest for some years in trying to benefit the children, and he had never asked Messrs. P. Walker and Sons. Ltd., to do anything for them without it had been acceded to with pleasure. lie had never met with any refusal or rebuff. He coupled with the toast, the name of Capten Potter. Captain A. F. G. Poirint in reaper hug said that on behalf of Messrs. P.Walker and Sons,Ltd., he was proud to be able to respond to the toast. In the first place,he I thought be could claim the proud position of being the eldest employe present. They had gone there to have an enjoyable time and they were keeping it up without any accidents. They had always had the pleasure of welcoming their friends' their official chiefs or heads of departments, end their friends in the railway departments. He had hi -rd a lot of talk about old-age pensions ; it would he rather a curious thing if there was an enquiry Trade as to how many private pensions were given by brewers. They had close on a hundred pensioners on their books. Mr. JOHN Wer.l3 said'that it gave him very great pleasure indeed to propose a toast, which he was sure would be very agreeable, and that was to propose the health of the visitors. He felt sure that he considered it a very high honour indeed, when they had gentlemen who would honour them with their presence at their annual picnic. He talieved that he was voicing their worthy chairman's opinion end that of the firm also, when he gave a very hearty welcome to those gentlemen I who had hondbml them with their presence. He hoped Oat the visitors would be spared many years to come, and be coupled with the toast the name of Aldhnnan Tinnier). . _

Aldernm TINNION replying, said that he thanked them very sincerely for the hearty manner in which the toast had been received. Unfortunately they had had that day the clerk of the weather against them. Looking at the faces of the employees and the visitors they at any rate seemed to have enjoyed themselves. Mr. TOWNLEY then spoke on behalf of the railway set vents. , _ . .

Mr.JoHN LEE next proposed a toast to the chairman, and Councillor Fulton-Smith in replying said that he thanked them very much ihdeed for the way in which the toast had been received. He certainly, felt that Messrs. P. Walker and Sons, Limited, was to im his life, for be devotad his whole life to them. Everything be did, he did with the best of motives. Be had laid demo his life to deal straightforwardly and if be tbst was the weakness of human nature for which be was not resporsible. Ho hoped that no one would point a finger to enyono of them, as having failed to do their duty to the firm. The last it= was "Auld Lang Syne " mid two veises were song with vest heartiness. Though the excursionists' pleasure was marred some- what by the rain, they all seemed to have had a good time. Warrington was reached at 12 midriglat.

PA.RISII Counn.—A meeting of the Parish Council took place on Monday evening at 8 o'clock in the new Council school, Stock-lane. Dr. Murray, J.P. occupied the chair and there were nbo present :—Messrs. J. G. Withinshaw, D. Houghton. J. Woodward, R. Routledge and Mr. E. Foster (clerk). The clerk opened tne meet- ing by reading the minutrs of last meeting which were passed as correct. A statement of accounts was pre - sented showing a balance in 'rind of £2 Os. 2d. and from this amount accounts were passed to be paid amounting to £1 Is. id.

div.head: Warrington Leather Thefts.
div.p: Warrington Leather Thefts.

Charles Steele (19), tube-turner, pleaded guilty (1) to warehouse-breaking at Warrington on May 25 and stealing eight bends ( f leather, the property of Randall Brothers, Limited ; and (2) stealing six bends of leather from the same warehouse en April JO, detection of the offence later in date having led to the discovery of the earlier. John Maginn (21), labourer, pleaded guilty to a share in both the offences. Frederick Br. .mfield (21), shca - repairer, pleaded guilty to a share in the offence of May 25, and George Ellis (21), labourer, to a share in the offence of April N. All the four plisoners had been incarcerated awaiting trial for seven weeks. Steele was sent to gaol for a month, and Ellis (a gainst whom there were four previous convictions) for four mouths. The other two prisoners were bound over for a year under the Probation Act.
EXCITING RACECOURSE SCENE.

At the Earlestown Police Court, on Monday' Arthur Flint, of Loncion,*was charged with stealing aR.S note froth Walter Longbotham, of Bungles, at Haydock Park 11 races, on Saturday. Detective-Sergeant Sutton's sus- picions were aroused by the movements of a gang in the shilling ring just before the second race, and he had them watched. The gang surrounded a men who was making s bet, and it was altered that the accuped extracted a purse from the man's hip pocket. The detective at once arrested Flint, and although the rest of the gang kicked and badly mauled the officer in an attempt to release accused, he stuck to his prisoner until he received assistance. In the struggle the purse was lost. The accused was taken to the racecourse police station, and in addition to Lii in gold a £5 note was found on him. The latter was afterwards claimed by Walter Longlxrtham, who said it had been stolen from his hip pocket the same afternoon. The accused was remanded to Warrington on Monday next.

-- National Decadence—ls it Avoidablb ? Sir,—One sometimes hears the question discussed, if Great Britain's Empire will ultimately share the fate of those Empires of the past which have declined. Mr. Balfour in a lecture given some time ago on "National Decadence" seemed to imply that decadence was" mere debilitation by process of time." The Roman Empire is singled out as an example, and the question concern- ing us is if modern states in general and Great Britain in particular should learn from the Roman Emp:re to expect and acquiesce in a period of decrepitude and an ultimate dissolution no more to be avoided than old age or death are to be avoided by the Individual? The Roman Empire was a premature attempt to establish a world polity undertaken in ignorance of the fundamental conditions of the problem. The *omens bad great organising genius, and borrowed their philosophic and aesthetic culture from Greece, then set to work to spread through the Mediterranean basin the civilisation thus compounded. When they were on the crest of their wave of prosperity no doubt they thought 311 was well. The surf of hostility seemed to break innocuous on the coast-line of their home. We to-day, wise after the event can see that their Static ideal was impossible in the nature of things. Why did not the Roman Empire expand until Equatorial Africa felt its power ? Because its system of organization was ODO which necessarily, weakened from the centre outwards. Because its method, its art, as Virgil called it was "paths impovere morem "—to impose a social order which was welcome no doubt, to certain of those classes sub- jected to it, but which had in it no principle of progress, of development, in a word, of life. This social order was vitiated by slavery and every sort of economic injustice ; and whilst here and there a wise adminis- trator might reform this or that abuse, scarcely anyone conceived the inspiriting possibility of a general and cumulative betterment of the whole body politic. We can scarcely point out an analogy between the Roman Empire and any modern State, as the former was not a State at all, but a world. It was not one political organism among many, but a cosmos suspended in chaos. It fell back to chaos for lack of light. It had no sane /political ideal. We to-day are applying cumulative knowledge, acquired through methodic investigation, to e hundred problems which the Romans tackled with the crudest empiricism, or not at all. We may fairly hope that the destiny of our modern State is to merge into am higher order, than lapse into decrepitude and dissoln- tion. As long as we have truth and mutual right as guides we must evolve into something better. Professor Lecky says one of the chief elements of British power is the moral prestige behind it, Mr. Asquith at the recent Pan-Anglican Conference pleaded for a better mutual understanding among men. We are in advance of our ancestors with regard not merely to our own rights but to the rights of others. If our national ideal is that " Righteousness which exalteth a nation " our path shall be upward and onward. We shall tread on the stepping stones of our dead selves to higher spheres of action and being. Yours etc., T.F.

div.head: LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: LIBERAL CLUB.
DISTRIBUTION OF BILLIARD PRIZES.

The prizes gained in the Christmas and spring billiard handicaps at the Liberal Club were distributed in the reading room on Wednesday evening by Captain G. R. Crosfield. Alderman Tinnion presided over a large attendance which included Mr. T. Pemberton (hon. secretary), and Councillor J. T. Locker (laon- secretary of the Liberal Association.) The CHAIRMAN expressed the regret of the members that Mr. A. H. Crosfield could not be with them but said they were pleased to have such a worthy representa- tive as Captain Crosfield. They owed the heartiest thanks to Mr. A. H. Crosfield for the handsome manner in which he had provided the prizes not only on that occasion but on many others and they were indebted to him for the very keen interest he took in everything appertaining to the success of that club. (Applause.) Mr. Crosfleld believed in recreation heart and soul, as being one of those things which brought out the better and finer qualities of a man. It was certain that if a man played games fairly and squarely he would be equally honest and straightforward in the game of life. (Applause.) Captain CROSFIELD said he could assure them he appreciated the honour they had done him in asking him who for the present was quite outside party I politics—he did not wish to be regarded as a party man I at all—to come to that club which represented so I much energy and self-sacrifice for the good of the. many ' causes which he knew the members had at heart. Captain Crosfield expressed the opinion that they ought to do more for the women in the matter of recreation as we owed more to them than was perhaps realized. History owed an immense amount to women but because their work was not done in the glare of the footlights it was apt to be overlooked. Continuing Captain Crosfield said they could not ask him to come there without expecting him to dwell, if only for a few moments, on the cause which he was convinced was of the highest consequence to every man, woman and child in this country—universal obligatory military training. He was afraid he could almost imagine a shiver going down some of his Radical friends' backs when be *mentioned the word obligatory, or to put it still more strongly, compulsory. He, however, ventured to suggest to them that it was, after all, the only fair and manly way for each one to do his little bit and not to expect the few to bear the burden and host of the day. He suggested that if they had all gone through the training referred to they would be able to play their games with a much greater sense of peace and security and they would enjoy them all the more when they had the feeling that they bad all done their duty by their country. Captaia Crosfield concluded by congratu- lating the members on the very successful competition they had had and the prize winners upon their victories. (Applause). Captain Crosfield then presented the prizes as follows :—Christmas Handicap :-1, gold albert, Coun- cillor J. T. Locker; 2, egg frame and spoons, M. Tobin ; 3, signet ring, S. W. Jeffrey ; 4, timepiece, G. Baker •, 5, dressing case, H. Hayes ; 0, biscuit barrel, A. Greenkalsh ; 7, sardine dish, W. H. Dutton, jour. ; 8, cigarette case, W. Furness; 9, pepperettes, J. Halliwell ; i 10, pepperettes, J. D. Brimelow ; 11, sugar end cream, H. Bunch ; 12, barometer, C. Caird ' • 13, case of carvers, G. Strange ; 14, jam dish, W. Whittaker ; 15, toast ' rack, G. Simpson ;16, pepperettes, r. Locker. Spring Handicap :-1, clock, F. Mallery ; 2, egg frame, S. Jakeman ; 3, pendant, P. Chambers ; 4, cruet, J. Curry; 5, teapot, H. Daintith ; 6, sugar basin and tongs, A. Robertson ; 7, pkkle jar, J.Davies ; 8, decanters, G. Howard. Councillor LOCKER, in moving n vote of thanks to Captain Crosfield,said be believed Radicals had at heart the safeguarding of the country quite as sincerely as Captain Cros field. They might have different modes of carrying that into effect, but for his own part he was a sound believer in the principles expounded by Captain Crosfield. The finest thing that coulrt be done for our Tenths was that they should be trained in rifle shooting. _lt was the ambition of all the members of that club to win the Crosfield billiard and bowling handicaps and he (Councillor Locker) was proud to have pulled off the "double event." (Laughter and applause). Mr. S. W.Jr.eartny seconded and said they must all be impressed by Captain Crosfield's enthusiasm in the Cause be had so warmly at heart. All the members of the club appreciated very much the efforts the Crosfleld family had put forward to make that club a strong resort of ardent Liberals. Captain Crosfield had not yet seen his way to step out on the pathway of Liberalism bat they hoped he would scot] do so and that he would not devote all his energies to one calve. (Applause). The CHAIRMAN endorsed Mr. Jeffrey's view. Pro- bably the result of Captain Crosfleld's work would be that the harvest would be gathered sooner than he anticipated. Let them hope the dream of his life might be realized early and that he would be able to devote his energies to some other equally important cause. (Applause.) The vote was accorded with great enthusiam. In responding Captain CROSFIELD said he was not quite as optimist/6 as the Chairman evidently was about the question, and because of the seriousness of the position he felt bound to devote his energies to the work he had taken in hand.

div.head: Billing—Daunt.
div.p: Billing—Daunt.

St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey, was the scene of a very pretty wedding on Tuesday afternoon when Mr. Peter Eric Billing, of Clifton,Bristol, was married to Miss Alice de Tracy Daunt, daughter of the late Mr. Arthur Kingscote Daunt and adopted niece of the Misses Tinsley, The Elms, Penketh. Great interest was taken in the happy event, the bride being well- known and esteemed in the district, and a large and fashionable congregi,tion assembled. The Rev. R. J. Bryant, BA., of St. Allaltis, Birmingham, performed the ceremony, assisted by the Rev. J. R. Jones, M A., vicar. The hymns " Lead us, heavenly Father, lead us" and "Now thank we all our God" were sung. Miss M. Standish was at the organ and played appropriate music, including Mendelssohn's Wedding March. The bride was escorted up the aisle by Mr. William Tinsley and was given away by Miss Tinsley. She I was charmingly attired in an Empire dress of old lace I worn by her grandmother and the veil was of white net, with motif Honiton lace, surmounted with a wreath of white heather. Her jewellery consisted of pearl ear-rings and an opal pendant, the gifts of the bridegroom, and she carried a lovely bouquet of lilies of the valley, also the gift of the bridegroom. There were five bridesmaids : —Miss Nancy Jackson, Miss Hartley, Miss Billing, Miss Muriel Tinsley and Miss Doris Ainley, who wore pretty dresses of cream spot net, trimmed with pale blue, and spot net hats bound with small pink and blue flowers. The bouquets were I composed of pink erica forget-me-nuts and gypsofole, and their ornaments were silver repouge pendants, set with a ruby, the gifts of the bridegroom. Ur. B. H. Hartley discharged the duties of best man. After I the ceremony, a reception was held at the Elms, a ' large number of guests attending. Photographs of the wedding party were taken by Mr. Birtles. Later the happy couple left for London, the.bride's travelling dress being of navy blue voile, trimmed with Oriental embroidery, with tuscan hat trimmed with roses, and blue feather boa. div.head: Pitt-Pitt.
div.p: Pitt-Pitt.

A. large congregation assembled in Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Thursday afternoon on the occa- sion of the marriage of Mr. Hadley John Pitt, Abbotts Ann, Andover, son of the late Mr. Walter Pitt, to Miss Mabel Pitt, daughter of the Rev. Sidney Pitt (superintendent minister of the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit), Bewsey Manse, Warrington. Great interest was taken in the ceremony, the bride being generally I esteemed in the town, and especially by those associated with the work of the Wesleyan Church in this circuit. The Rev. Sidney Pitt (father of the bride) and the ' Rev. J. T. Gurney, were the officiating ministers. The hymns The voice that breathed o'er Eden" and "0 Perfect Love" were sung, and Mr.:T. W. Pearce who presided at the organ played appropriate selections, the bridal party leaving the church to the familiar strains of Mendelssohn's Wedding Marah. The bride, who wasl given away by her father, was charmingly attired in embroidered Nina de sole, trimmed with silk lace and white satin, with Brussels net veil, trimmed with Honiton lace, and surmounted with a wreath of white heather. She carried a handsome bouquet of white roses, tuba roses, maidenhair fern and smilax. She was attended by four bridesmaids : The Misses Lois, Theo, and Daisy Pitt (sisters of the bride), and Miss Darcy M. Pitt (sister of the bridegroom). The two elder brides- maids wore green voile dresses, trimmed with cream lace and dark green velvet, and hats of cream straw, trimmed with pink roses and green velvet. Their bouquets were composed of pink car- nations. The two younger bridesmaids were attired in white mousseline de sois with pink mousseline de soie hats, and carried bouquets of sweet peas. All wore- neckleis, the gifts of the bridegroom. The Rev. E. Utley Tuck discharged the duties of best man. 'After the wedding a reception was held in the Lecture IHall and was attended by about 100 guests. Later the happy couple left for Llandudno where the honey- ' moon will be spent. The bride's travelling dress was a green tweed costume, with satin-straw hat, trimmed I with chiffon and green velvet. div.head: MR. CROSFIELD, M.P. CHAMPIONS THE POSTMEN. A Wages question in the House of Commons.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD, M.P. CHAMPIONS THE POSTMEN. A Wages question in the House of Commons.
SPEECH BY THE MEMBER.
HOUSE OF COMMO&S, THURSDAY.

The House went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates. On the vote for the Post, office, Mr. Buxton (Postmaster General) made a general review of the work of the year. He stated that the 'revenue amounted to 221 millions and the expenditure to 182 millions, showing a surplus of rather more than n millions. The estimate for the present year was roughly 23 millions of revenue and 191 millions of expenditure.

div.head: POST-OFFICE AS EMPLOYER.
div.p: THE POST-OFFICE AS EMPLOYER.

He reminded the Committee that the Post-office is a great employer of labour, and re-affirmed his view that such a department ought to set a good example to other employers. Last Christmas he was able to raise the wages for casual labour from 20s. to 21s. a week, and the results showed that this was a good investment of public money. He was endeavouring to dearwith the question of sweating, and had appointed an inspector of contracts as a step in the direction he desired to go. In regard to the position of Post-office servants, be referred to the new classification under which some offices had "gone down," and expressed his regret that a circular issued to members on behalf of the employees should give the impression that the reduced scale would apply to existing postmen in those offices, the fact being, he said, that no existing Post-office servant should lose either in the scale or in status. Any alteration' he said, would apply only to new entrants. Moreover, the vast majority of offices benefited by the arrangemenl.He was still open to argument as to whether any par- ticular office had been unjustly treated, and where the unit of work or the cost of living was shown not to be correct the scale would be open to revision. As to the general relations of the Post-office with its servants, he reminded the Committee that he had recognised the representative character of the great postal associations, and said he bad never regretted doing so. On the whole, he held that this great public department was a striking testi- mony to the efficiency and loyalty of its servants. (Cheers.)
THE NEW CLASSIFICATION. CRITICISNIS AND COMPLAINN.

Dr. Rtftherford (L —Brantford) warmly congratu- lated the Postmaster General ,on the many reforms he had introduced and on the success of his administra- tion. As regarded the postmen, however,he complained of anomalies in the new classification. In Chiswick,for instance, the pay was 335. and in Brantford 2,55., although the cost of living was practically the same. He urged that the postal aral of London should be extended so as to include all districts within a twelve- mile radius. To call attention to these matters he moved a reduction of the vote. * ' Mr. Walsh (Lab.—lnce), said it was a serious matter that such a large number of offices should be degraded from their former status. He reminded the Committee that the present scale of wages was fixed in 1890, and thatsince then the cost of living and of house rents had materially increased. The new entrants would begin in the Wigan office with a minimum is. 6d. less than and a maximum 2s. less than existing employds. Reductions would take place also in such towns as Oldham, St. Helens, Warrington, Wolverhampton, and Clitheroe. The State, he• held, should be a model employer, and by stopping the practice of giving various kinds of work out to contract should be more and raore a direct employer as well. Sir J. F. Lease (L—Accrington) asked whether he was not right in assuming that the scheme was not laid down as a hard-and-fast rule, and that on good cause being shown the Postmaster General would re-con- sider it.

I Mr. A. 11. Crosfield (L —Warrington) stated that in that town the minimum rate would be 17s. and the maximum 253. The minimum rate would therefore be [less than what was paid locally to labourers, and the I ma•xuntam,after the shilling reduction that was proposed, would be little more than what was paid to builders' labourers. He had always felt that labourers deserved quite as much consideration as any other part of the working class, and he would be more than sorry, even by way of illustration, to say one ward in disparage- ment—trf them. But one had to consider that in the postal service, besides an irreproachable character, a certain position had to be kept up. It was certain tha t of late years there had been an increase in the cost of living,and for the life of him he could not see any reason for a redaction being made. (Cheers.) Thanks to the invariable ceurtesy.of the Postmaster-General, he had had the opportunity of mentioning these matters to him privately, and he had hoped they might be mon. sidered, because, as he had assured the right hon. gentleman, there was a very strong feeling on the sub. ject. (Cheers.) Without enlarging on the general question, Mr. Crosfield added that while, of course, an endeavour must be made to hit the happy mean, nobody felt more strongly than he did that too often people still failed to recognise the advantageous results which were to be got by maintaining a fair remuneration and giving proper attention to the hours of labour. He trusted the whole subject would receive the careful attention of the Postmaster General. (Cheers). At nine o'clock over twenty members had addressed the Committee, the burden of the speeches of nearly all of them being the reductions proposed to be made in the wages of plstal servants in the constituencies the members represented, and that either because of the cost of living or the quality of work done no such reduction ought to take place.

div.head: -MR. BUXTON'S REPLY.
div.p: -MR. BUXTON'S REPLY.

Mr. Buxton said with regard to the discussion on classification, if anyone knowing nothing of the matter had listened to the debate he would have been led to belieye that the Postmaster General had put down the wages of every ex,stinz and every future postman. IWhat were the facts ? Taking the offices as a whole and the sub-olices as a whole, under the proposal of the Cammittee, as madified by himself, with the assent of the Treasury, there would be an increase in the case of postmen's wages in 4,f300 offices and a diminutlon in '7so—about one in- six.in only five of the offices in London would a reduction take place. If a pima facia case could be made out in regard to any particular town the Board of Trade were quite willing to reconsider their decision. He had endeavoured to carry out the classification to the best of his ability on a fairand jPst basis. A certain number of places were bound to be affected adversely. But, as he had explained, the vast majority of places would benefit. He was not open to reconsider the whole basis of classification, hut he was perfectly willing to recon- sider any particular Case, either as to the volume of work or as to the cost of living, if material facts were brought before him. (Cheers.) Mr.. Seddon (I.lb.—Nearton) asked for an assurance that postal servents,who Were members of the Territorial force, would not have to make good out of their own pockets any difference between their own wages and the wages of their substitutea during training. Dr. Rutherford offered to withdraw his amendment, but the Opnesition objected, and the discussion was continued till 11, when progress was reported.

Fined for Assault.

At the 'Warrington Police Court yesterday, Harry Eornand, lodging at the Twiggery Farm, was sum- moned for assaulting James Harrtson, 326, Manchester- road, on Saturday, 11th inst. Mr. C. H. Unswortb,for the complainant, said that on Saturday night Mr. Harrison along with his wife were returning home from the market when they were met by the defen- ant, with whom they had previously had an altercation. He struck complainant behind the ear, knocking him to the groun d.—The maglstrates imposed a fine of 10s. and costs, Xi. Ds.

div.head: ISLE OF MAN RECORD PASSAGE.
div.p: THE ISLE OF MAN RECORD PASSAGE.

The new Isle of Man turbine steamer Ben-my-Chree, which left Liverpool for Douglas on Wednesday morn- ing, against a strong tide, made the passage from the Mersey Bar to Victoria Pier in 2 hours 19 minutes, or about 241 knots per hour. Her engineer is confident she will yet do the passage at 2G knots.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.
Local cricketers had an enforced rest on Saturday,the persistent rain necessitating the abandonment of all matches.

The Warrington Works Competition continues to arouse great interest. On Tuesday evening Pearson and Knowles pulverised Richmond's,fo: after compiling 111 for the loss of only 4 wickets they had no difficulty in sending the gas stove men to the right-about for the insignificant total of 25. P. and K. had the assistance of Mr. James Dodds who, however, did not go to the wicket bat did some smart work in the field. A fine partnership between Thompson and W.Bennett realized 82 runs, Bennett being the first to leave with 40 to his credit, while Thompson knocked up 53. Bennett also captured fivWwickets for ten runs.

-- -- The members of Mr. Down's bands are not only enthusiastic musicians but know how to play cricket well. On Tuesday afternoon they played Warrington Thnrsday and defeated them by a majority of 79. The visitors had two flue batsmen in 3. Hackney and W. H. Podmore who made 69 and 50 respectively before carrying out their bats. Warrington Thursday, could make little headway against the bowling of W. H. Pod- more and W. Howard, their top scorer being E. White who made 25.

-- Mr. Podmore was presented with a gold-centred medal, suitably engraved, and given by Mr. Down for his destructive bowling and spirited batting. The bandsmen were captained bv Mr. Robert Lowe, and the Thursday team by Mr. T.G. Bate. After the match the teams sat down to an excellent tea given by Mr. Down which was presided over by Alderman Forshaw, president of the Warrington Club, •-,iho was al-imparted by Mr. Down and the respective captains.—ln respond- ing to a vote of thanks Mr. Down said bath he and Mrs. Down took a great interest in all matters con- nected with the members of the bands. He had thoroughly enjoyed the match and hoped to have many more. Cheers were given for Mr. and Mrs. Dawn, accompanied by musical honours.

Bowling. Saturday last was a red letter day, in the annals of Forestry when a goodly number of Foresters journeyed to the Stamford Arms, Bollington, on the occasion of the first bowling handicap and picnic promoted by the Warrington District of the Order. A good sprinkling of the District officers including Bros. W. R. Smith, D.C.R., J. Walsh, D.S.C.R., L.Davies, D.S., P. Peacock, D. T. E., Clayton, W. Hipkiss, J. Chrimes, j. Davies and J. Thornley accompanied the party who were conveyed by Mr. H. F. Greenough's buses. The weather was far from what was desired but after a capital tea which was tabled in Host Jeffersoies best style, the weather having in the meantime improved, the bowling was proceeded with.

-- The novices were soon wending their way blcic with the balbnces on their scoring cards to debit, and then some really good games_ were witnessed, the final between Bro. Bennett of Court 431 and Bro. Clare of Court 430 ending in Bro. Bennett winning 11-10, being particularly exciting.

The members then adjourned to the Billiard Room, where under the presidency of Bro. W. R. Smith, D.C.R., the prizes were dtstritnited amongst the winners amidst much enthnsiasm. The 16 prize-winners were respectively Bros. Bennett, Clare, Cunningham, Stock- ton. Higginson, Whalley, Hill, Berry, Hughes, TJnsworth, Andron, Goulding, Howard, Houghton, Small and Baines. A pleasing feature of the picnic WAS that all the prizes were presented by the officers and workers of the District.
-- The Warrington Works Competition will be resnmed to-day when the following matches will be played : SECOND ROUND,
Castle Robber v. Wbiteoross No. 2 L. & N.-W. v. Crosdeld's No. 1 TIIIR,D ROUND.

--- Lancashire and Cheshire made no mistake in their match against Staffordshire on Saturday and piled on a majority of 145 points. Four Warrington players assisted their county and two of them were victorious, A. Scott (Cemetery) beating H. Harley (Old Oak) by 21-17, and A, Greave (Bull's Head) accounting for A. Ashton (Central) by 21-14. G. Ball. jun. (Cemetery) went down before F. Mason (Pyle Cock) to the ertent of 14-21, and T. Mae!) (Cemetery) had the hard luck to be beaten by W. R. Baker (Oaklands) by 21-20.

Sam Sackville (Swinton), the Lancashire and Cheshire Amateur champion of 1907, carried off the honours of the day by winning the L. and C. Association's gold medal, awarded for the best aggregate in these country games. He has uot sustained a defeat in county games this season. •

-7 • Daring the progress of the match the magnificent silver challenge cup presented to the British Crown Green Association by its patron, Mr. A. 11. Crosfield, M.P., of Warrington, WII3 on view in the pavilion at the Red Lion Rotel, Withington. Lancashire and Cheshire's magnificent victory over Staffordshire-291 on the aggregate—makes them strong favoorites for the Crosfield Cup.

-- Warrington Municipal Guild visited Altrincham and were beaten by St. goorge's team by 39 on the singles and 41 on the doubles. Warrington C. and B. club entertained Seaforth and wets victorious by 31 points. On the home and home matches, however, Seaforth have a majority of 17.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

- - The Warrington Cycling Club paid their annual visit to Beeston Towers, the home of their President, on Saturday last, the weather—which was anything but conducive to riding—compelling the members to make the journey by train, only one of the number braving the elements and completing the distance by road. A most enjoyable time was spent in spite of Mid unfavour- able conditions, a capital musical programme adding to the enjoyment of the fifty odd present. A small section of the members afterwards travelled on to Farndon, to spend the week-end where they were joined by others on the Sunday morning.

Tuesday evening saw the return visit to Glazahury carried out, only a small muster putting in an appear- ance. For the second week in succession further progress in the bowling handicap has been prevented by rain. About thirty members turned up at Sankey on Wednes- day evening in the hope of snatching a game; the enthusiasm shown by the members for these fixtures has been one of the features of the season.
To-day the Cluh ply another visit to the picturesque little village of Hale.

div.head: Water Polo.
div.p: Water Polo.
On Wednesday night Warrington visited Everton and played a rare gams, in fact spectators say the game of their life. What rare talent Warrington possess is plainly visible by this match.

-- As was only proper that veteran W. Ashton scored th 3 only goal although other players had hard lines. Woods in goal was a marvel. Everton could not get the ball past him and the equalizing goal caught his fingers before going through. The forward trio of Wolstencroft, Pemberton and Allen can only be seen to be believed. They played without one fault.
Warrington have not done very badly so far this season. There record is won two, lost two and drawn one. Not at all a bad record and more ;sinning matche3 to follaw !

Rugby Football. A meeting in connection with the newly-formed Warrington and District l unior Rugby League (affiliated to the Northern Union ill be held on the Warrington Football ground next Tuesday at 8 o'clock. Mr. H. Ashton will preside, and all the clubs are invited to send representatives. The business will include the appoint- ment of committee, &c.

div.head: CYCLISTS AT BRESTON.
div.p: CYCLISTS AT BRESTON.
Ladles' Day.

There is no doubt that the most popular fixture of the year in connectioo with the Warrington Cycling Club is the visit to the picturesqmely situated retreat of the esteemed president, Mr. John Naylor, Beeston Towers. Himself an enthusiastic cyclist, Mr. Naylor is never happier than when entertaining fellow- wheelers, and an outing at Beeston is one of the most delightful. experiences Imaginable. On the occasion of the Warrington Cycling Club's visit there is always a large muster of the fair sex —in fact the day is known as "Ladies' Day." It was unfortunate that "Ladies' Day" of 1908,—Saturday,- last—was not favoured by the weather. During the afternoon rain fell almost incessantly and the result was that the visitors were deprived of the pleasure of the cycle ride through the far-famed Delamere Forest which at this time of the year is looking at its best. Members and their lady friends, altogether to the number of about 50, left Bank Quay Station either by the 1.50 or 2 p.m. trains. 0 .ving to the poor train service to Beeston an hour and a half had to be spent in Chester, and as rain continued to fall the visitors ivhiled away the time by an inspection of the shops in the -Rows or a visit to the Cathedral, but at 4.14 all went by the train to Beeston, the Towers being reached a few minutes before five o'clock. They were met in the drive by Mr. and Mrs. Naylor and family, who accorded them an exceptionally hearty welcome. By this time the rain had, ceased, but the beautiful grounds were saturated and outdoor games were an impossibility. After an inspection of Mr. Naylor's charming residende, the visitors sat down to an excellent tea. Amongst others present were Mr. and Mrs. Henshall, Sergeant-Major Dalmage (captain of the club),llr. T. P. Throssell (sub-captain), Mr. F. Garnett (hon. treasurer), Mr. J. T. Sampson (hon. secretary), Messrs. W. C. Litton and B. Podnaore (lion, auditors), and the following members of the committee : —Meesrs. H. Smith, A. Fieldhouse, J. B. Poole and W. Taylor. After tea photographs of the visitors were taken on the lawn by Mr. B. Jones. of Warrington. after which all assembled in the handsome billiard-room for the usual concert. Sergt.-Major Delmage presided. A high-class programme was submitted, and was much appreciated. The first item, a song entitled " Roses," was well rendered by Mr. Fieldhouse, whose baritone voice was heard to great advantage. Miss Nellie Anderton (contralto) gave an artistic Interpretation of "She wandered down the mountain side." A vociferous encore was the result, and she charmed all her hearers with The sweetest flower that blows." Mr. Poole also had the honour of a recall for his singing of "Bedouin love song." He later cantribated, also in good style, "Oh I oh ! hear the wild wind blow." Mr. Fieldhouse sang " The little Irish girl " most pleasingly and the concert, concluded with an effective rendering by Miss Anderton of " 13y the fountain." Mr. George Anderton was the accompanist. Sergeant-Major Delmaee in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. and lairs.v Naylor for their hospitality. said it was evident how much the visitors had all enjoyed themselves and Mrs. Naylor must feel that there had been no lack of effort on the part of the visitors to show their appreciation of the many good things which, with her usual kindly forethought, she had provided. He thanked Miss Anderton and those gentlemen who had so materially contributed to the enjoy:neat, and hoped they might all have the pleasure of listening to them on many similar auspicious occasions. (Applause). Mr. Sampson, in seconding the motion, said he could assure Mr. and Mrs. Navfor that they looked forward to this annual visit with much pleasure. He would remind the ladies that it was " President's Day " a fortnight hence, and on behalf of the club be extended to Mr. and Mrs. Naylor a hearty welcome to Sandi way. The visit that day had added another to the long list of pleasant memories of Beeston Towers. (Applause.) The resolution was carried with great heartiness and the singing of "For he's a jolly good fellow." Mr. Naylor replied on behalf of himself, Mrs. Naylor and the family, and said ha was always pleased to see the members of the club at Beeston Towers. Some of the members had told him In confidence that the bridge , at Warrington had not been widened yet—(laughter)— but he hoped there was a good time coming when the , Corporation of Warrington would make it easier and less dangerous for the inhabitants, and cyclists in particular, to get out into the country. (Laughter and applause.) At times the bridge at Bridge-foot was a London Bridge on a smaller scale, and the traffic was so great that a cyclist could not cross it with safety.. He had seen a report in the newspapers with reference to the footbridge it was proposed to erect over the river at,Howley. He wished that the Corporation, instead of carrying out that idea, would build a proper bridge, as, in his opinion, it would be a waste of money to put up a temporary structure. What they wanted was a permanent bridge to enable them to get through the Park into the Knutsford-road and thence into the country. Such a bridge would be a great boon to cyclists. At any rate he hoped the club would take care that the bridge was male available for cycles. (Applause.) Much amaseraent was caused at : this stage by Mr. Naylor's description of a recent motor car adventure. - -
The party then left to catch the 8.11 train for Mester, Warrington being reached in good time. The outing proved to be moat enjoyable, notwithstanding the adverse weather conditions.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPP3DROIE.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPP3DROIE.

Those who wish to see something extraordinary in animal trading should not miss this week's entertain- ment at the Palace and Hippodrome. Richard C)rbin's performing dogs submit a turn which is at once pleasing and unique. The most remarkable thing about it is that the trainer himself does not appear on the stage,and the dogs go through their perforthance as if spontaneously and without supervisions It is amusing to see g noodle climbing a step ladder with easy assurance, while another takes a barrel across the stage by rolling over and over inside it. Somer- saulting and high-jumping are other accomplishments of these surprisingly sagacious animals and their turn must be seen to be believed. Another capital feature of the programme is-J. F. Elliston's sketch" The Art of Deception" in which Shaun Glenville, as the tramp, is the leading figure. There is not a dull moment when he is on the stage and tbe audi- ence is kept in a state of merriment until the curtain falls. The Florias, novelty equilibrists and slack wire artistes, are experts in their line of busi- ness and fully deserve the applause with which their wonderful feats are received. The Avolos, too, present oiled the smartest acrobatic and gymnastic shows ever seen in Warrington. A little sketch " The Escapade" by Edie Casson and Alexander Wills gives further variety to the entertainment and it is admir- ably presented. A husband, anxious to spend the evening at a fancy dress ball,nresses his better half to go and see her dear mother. She appears to fall in with his idea and leaves the house,but in a short time changes her mind and returns. The sequel can be readily imagined, and it provides good fun. Victor Travers, eccentric comedian, finds much favour and Mavine Cannon is a popular comedienne. Les Belles Americaine are pleasing vocalists and expert dancers.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

The management announce a special attraction next week in the engagement of Miss Helen Roberts who will appear in the now famous Salome dance and Mendelssohn's " Spring Song " dances which have created such a sensation in the Metropolis. Harry Grey, the Australian nugget, who is said to be Australia's funniest comediamwill make his first appear- ance in Warrington. Other features of an excellent programme will be contributed by: —Professor Norton, sleight of hand expert; Los Zelovas, acrobatic equilibrists ; Ernest Rees, the popular London come- dian ; Robins and Collier, in their comedy railway station scene "The Lady and the Porter"; the Violas, white Mahatmas,in their wonderful silent transmission, Knight's tour and mental telegraphy (Hdlle. Viola will inform patrons as to the whereabouts of missing friends and relatives at each performance); Marjit3r Clarke and Percy Hayden in their musical comedy. "By Appointment." Miss Helen Roberts is only 17, but she has spent nine years at a dancing Academy at Milan, and her performances not only show that she has been well- trained, but that she has a keen taste for the highest branches of her art. Her representation of the famous Salome dance is exceedingly weird in char- acter, yet nevertheless is marked 'by a grace of move- ment which is fascinating to behold. Miss Roberta has delighted huge audiences wherever she has appeared and mach interest is being taken in her visit to Warrington.

div.head: Church Offered for Sale
div.p: Church Offered for Sale

The Presbyterian Church of St. John's, Warrington, was offered for sale by auction on Wednesday by Messrs. Thomas Sutton and Sons. The church, which is over 100 years old, is considered quite unsuitable for devotional worship. It occupies a site of 1,014 square yards, having a frontage on Winvvick-street. Mr. T. A. Sutton conducted the sale, and when the bidding had reached .C.,1,000 the property was with- drawn. If the building bad been disposed of, a new church, in all probability, would have been erected in the neighbourhood of Wilderspool.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
Last iffeek of Mr. Ryder Boys'
Season.

This is the last week of Mr. Ryder Boys' and his talented company's season here, and the programme is quite in keeping with the high standard 'which has been maintained during their Month's visit. On Monday and Tuesday evenings " David Garrick," that celebrated costume comedy which loses none of its fascination as years go by, was presented and gave great delight to the andienc3s. Mr. Leonard Mudie is to be congratulated upon a worthy portrayal of the title part. It was a fine piece of acting, evidencing histrionic powers of an unusually high order, and took the house by storm, Mr. Mudie being repeatedly applauded. He was seen at his best in the second, act , vllere he had to feign drunkenness and make himself generally obnoxious, in obedience to his undertaking to " cure " Violet Gresham of her love for him. Miss Elsie Vron was a charming Violet Gresham and won golden opinions. As Alderman Gresham, Mr. Ryder Boys had a part which suited him splendidly and he made the most of it. Mr. Henry Worrall gave further evidence of his versatility by a capital representation of the Hon. Tom Tallyhaut, and all the other parts were in capable hands.

On Wednesday and Thursday an early play by Pinero " The Money Spinner" was performed. The cast was not the strongest combination which Mr. Ryder Boys' company makes possible, but in the main, the essential impersonations were well done. The mast noticeable weakness was, however, one not dependent on the skill of the actors and actresses themselves but consisted of the faulty memorising of the parts with its consequent irritating recourse to the prompter's help. Mr. Murray Graham's " Lord Kengassie," Mr. L. Mudie's "Herold Boycott" and Miss E. Vron's "Millicent" deserve particular mention as careful and artistic specimens of the actor's art.

Last evening Mr. Harry Nicholl's great farce " Jane" was presented with success, Miss Betty Noel acquitting herself well in the title rOle. "Jane " will again be performed this evening and those who want to see 'something really laughable should certainly not i miss it. There s not a dull moment from beginning to end.
After this evening's performance the theatre will be closed for a fortnight for renovation and will open on August Bank Holiday „with a special London production.

div.head: Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society,
div.p: Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society,

- It has been decided to bold a picnic in connection with the above Society on Saturday, August 22nd. The rendezvous is the pretty Cheshire village of A-ton. Bridge. Not only members are invited but also their gentlemen or lady friends are to be welcomed. It is proposed to proceed to the destination by means of 'buses, waggonettes, &c. An excellent and interesting programme has been arranged. There will be sports, an al fresco concert, a cricket match between the " Council " and the "Rest of the House," and s bowling match between the ladies and the gentlemen. There is only fine weather needed to ensure a most enjoyable outing, though in case of wet weather an ample hall has been secured.

Warrington Man Convicted at Northwich. Thomas Snelson, a wiredrawer, of Warrington, and James Lomas, described as a stoker, of Manchester. who were remanded for inquiries at Nortbwich a weal,: ago on charge of stealing a pail- of men's boots, value 3s. 11d., the property of the Cash Boot Com- pany, because of Loraas's refusal to give any account of himself, again appeared before Messrs. J. W. Deakin (chairman) and T. B. Moretoa on Monday. The' magistrates were of opinion that Snelson had been led into trouble by Lomas. Lomas would there- fore have to go to gaol for two months' hard labour an& Snelson for one month with bard labour.

The judgment delivered by TRADE UNIONS Justice Channell this week AND TEM LAW, in the curious Trade Union case, in which a man on the Isick list had been fined by his Union for obeying the orders of his doctor, in contravention of the rules, is notable in several respects. First of all, it reminds us how recent is the legal recogni- tion of Trade Unions. The Court, said Justice Channel!, would be going contrary to the authorities if it ware to hold that prior to the Act of 1871 the Union in question would not have been held to be an illegal society. The year mentioned was that in which the first great, but far from satisfactory, Trade Union Act was passed. Unions of working men began to come into existence immediately on the repeal of the combination laws in 1625, but they existed in spite of the law, not under its sanction, and it was I not until 1876 that the powerful trade societies then in existence were able to wring from Parlia- ment what was henceforward known as "the workmen's charter." The tone of Justice CHANNELL'S remarks seems to have been curiously in keeping with the spirit which has led the judges on so many cases to whittle away the intentions of the Legislature, until it became necessary to re-affirm them through the recent Trades Disputes Act. It is assumed, for instance, that trade unions exist mainly for fighting purposes. This may be said to agree with the legal definition which describes them as ,‘ continuous associations of wage-earners for the purpose of maintaining or improving the con- ditions of their employment." But it is indis- putable that the Unions spend much less money on strikes than on objects of 'a purely beneficent nature. This has been the case throughout their whole career. When the National Federation of Employers was formed in 1873 it was stated in documents issued by that body that the Amalgamated Society of Engineers had spent in one year considerably over a hundred thousand pounds in trade disputes. It was easy, however, to prove from the books of the Society that only a little over £ll,OOO had been so expended, the remainder of the large sum having been paid out in sick pay, out-of-work allowances, and other benefits. The Amalgamated Society of Engineers was then, and now is, the strongest of existing Trade Unions. But the experience of both great and small societies has been much the same. Far the largest portion of their funds has gone in relief of the poor rates. In 1673, the Employers' Federation seems to have known as little of the internal working of the Trade Unions as most of our judges have done both then and since. It spoke in the manifestoes which it issued at that time of the large sums of money at the disposal of the Union officials, and of the considerable salaries that were paid to them. Yet there was no Trade Union official who was then paid more than £250 a year, nd there was only one who received a salary of this magnitude. In general, a Trade Union secretary received a wage of a week, which, by the way, was the sum paid to Mr. Thomas Burt up to the time when he entered Parliament. GEORGE ODGER was paidhalf-a-crown a week as the Secre- tary of the London Trades Council, a position which had previously been filled by M 7. GEORGE Ilowere. for no payment at all. Most employers of labour nowadays hold very different opinions of Trade Unions and their officials from those which were entertained by their predecessors of thirty- five years since. Experience has proved to thorn that Trade Union secretaries are, as a rule, much more actively employed in preventing strikes than in fermenting them. Tbey are not always able to • get their way, and they are often in trouble with their members because they prefer the way of peace. The :latest striking instance of this is the case of Mr. GEORGE N. BAnNzs, M.P., who has resigned his post because the Engineers in the North would not follow the advice that he gave to them. It is as oddly wrong to picture the Trade Union secretary as an originator of strife as to suppose that Trade Unions exist solely beeause workmen want to fight their employers.
